speechtext: The statement that we have hundreds of these boats is about as exaggerated .as many others made by the hon. *member. We have engaged only such boats as were absolutely necessary for defence purposes.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: Tell the committee how many.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: The hon. member asks that the female relations of men who have been enrolled and enlisted in the navy up to the present time only shall have votes. I do not know what view the Secretary of State or the other members of the Government would take of that suggestion, but I do say it would be doing great injustice, as we are still enlisting men and sending them everywhere-

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: Yes, hiring boats.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: -we are still enlisting men and sending them overseas. When they go overseas they go on vessels of the British navy which are engaged in work of the most important and dangerous description.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: I was not finding fault with the men who go overseas but with the men who stay in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: A provision restricting this right to the relatives of men who have already enlisted would have no appreciable effect; it would not vary conditions to the extent of ten votes. Between now and next spring few if any boate will be chartered or purchased by the Government of Canada, and I do not think that my hon. friend's suggestion would make a particle of difference to the vote which will take place in a few months.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
Then show your good
faith by making the change.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: I would have no objection to doing so, only there might be cases where grave injustice would be caused.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: Does not the patrol service extend up the St. Lawrence and the Great Lakes ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman will
understand how undesirable it would be to discuss the patrol service in the House; but we shall be glad to give him, as a member of Parliament, all information at any time.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
'What is the
name of the boat referred to and what department is she employed?

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
I think it is the Helena. She is employed .by the Customs Department.
With regard to men who have enlisted for service, I know that in Halifax there are
some forty men, masters and mates, who were engaged by the Department of Naval Affairs as far back as June to take charge of patrol boats. These boats have not yet been supplied, and .still these men are drawing pay and living .at the Acadian hotel which has been taken over by the department as a boarding house for them. They have done nothing except to go out for an hour or two each day in Halifax harbour for instruction in mine-sweeping. Will their female relatives be entitled to vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: Those men are enrolled and enlisted and belong to the naval forces of Canada. They are going on boats that will be ready in a very short time, the construction of which has been delayed. As soon as the boats are ready these men will be engaged in a very important and arduous work. Their time is not being wasted at Halifax as they are receiving instruction which will be of great value when they take up their work. It was found that we could not safely put off their employment to a later date. They must he ready for duty the moment the boats are ready. Their female relatives would undoubtedly have the right to vote.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: I understand that there is quite a large waiting list of masters and mates who have applied for similar positions, so that I do not think there would have been much danger to the department if they had delayed making these appointments. Will the instructors on the Niobe at Halifax, who are giving instruction to the cadets and students at the naval college, be included in the naval forces, so that their female relatives will have the right to vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: If they are enrolled and enlisted as members of t'he naval service and are bound to serve during the period of the war, they will belong to the naval forces of Canada. I cannot tell my hon. friend, offhand, however, whether they are in that position or not. With regard to the masters and mates, their training has taken a somewhat longer time than we had anticipated, but that is something that could not possibly have been prevented. In Great Britain the highest value is attached to the services rendered by men of the mercantile marine, by fishermen, and others, who are engaged in mine-sweeping and other work of an important and dangerous character.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: The minister said that it would not be advisable to make public the information, asked for by the member for Bonaventure. Could the information be given privately?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman applies to the department the information will be given to him privately.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
Answers have been made to question put by hon. gentlemen in respect to matters affecting provinces other than Quebec. That province is referred to,in only one place, page 16.of the reprinted Bill. I quote from section 65A as amended:
1. In the provinces of Quebec, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick the enumerators shall adopt as the basis of the lists of voters which they respectively shall compile the lists prepared for the several polling divisions established, and which on the sixtieth day next preceding the day fixed for the nomination of candidates for the election were in force, or were last in force, under the laws of the province, for the purposes of provincial elections, and they shall not add to such basis list any other names than those of female voters qualified to vote by this part of this Act nor strike off nor erase therefrom any other names than those of persons disqualified from voting, by this part of this Act, and section 62 of this Act shall apply only to qualified female voters whose names do not appear on any list compiled by any enumerator and to persons whose names he has erased or struck from such basis list.
The Secretary of State has done some nice drafting in this Bill in providing for mushroom enumerators. Section 42 of the Dominion Elections Act, as amended by this Bill, is where the mushroom enumerator comes in. It reads:
Subject to the provisions of section 65a of this Act the Governor in Council may appoint enumerators in each province to make lists of the electors in each electoral district, and the returning officer of each electoral district shall assign one of such enumerators to each polling district therein.
Under one provision of the Bill it is provided that the enumerator shall adopt the old list as the basis for the making up of the new one, but this last provision seems to require him to make out new lists. Although it is provided that in the province of Quebec he shall take the old lists as a basis, it is further provided that he shall compile an entirely new list. I should like to have an explanation of that. I wrote to Hon. E. L. Patenaude, then Secretary of State, on June 6, asking 'him to send me a list of the electors of St. James Division, Montreal. On June 7 he wrote me a letter -I think it was 'his last communication as minister; he resigned on that day-enclosing the list I asked for. I find that St. James Division, Montreal, has 88 polling booths and 7,343 voters. That list includes outsiders, people who were bom in Ontario. It includes Jews who may be regarded by

the enumerator as persons of German birth, and who .may be, therefore, struck off the list. How is the enumerator to find out w.bat female electors should go on the list? How is he to find out how many soldiers iiave gone to the front from St. James Division? How is he to obtain information as to the wives, sisters and female relatives of these soldiers? I suppose he will take as a basis the list already existing, compile a new list, and send it to the returning officer. Who will revise this list that the enumerator has compiled? The basis of the list of electors in Quebec is by virtue of article 180 o,f the Election Act of Quebec, amended in 1912 and in 1915, so as to have the system of "one man one vote." Article 180 says:
The following persons, and no others, being males, and who at the time of the deposit of the list under articles 196 and 197, or 222 or
223,	as the case may be, are domiciled within the limits of the municipality for which the list is made, and who are of the full age of 2/1 years, subjects of His Majesty by birth or naturalization and not otherwise legally disqualified, shall be entered upon the list of electors.
The suffrage in Quebec is very wide. The franchise is given to sons of owners, occupiers or tenants, every man over 21 years of age who. has an average revenue of $10 per month. 11am not going to say anything about the rural districts. In the municipalities the list is made up by the secretary-treasurer of every village and deposited on the 15th of this month. The list is posted up, and if there is any objection, or if any one claims that his name should be put on, the municipal council deals with the matter. In the city of Montreal we are under article
224.	We make up the list every two years. Notice is given that those who have the necessary franchise shall appear and swear that they are entitled to vote. The list is made up in December. In January, notice is given that the Board of Revisors will go over the list and receive complaints as to errors. This board is created by virtue of article 224 of the Election Act, which says:
There shall be, for each of the cities of Montreal, Quebec and Three Rivers, a board of revision called the "Board of Revisors of the city of (name of the city)." The said hoard shall be composed of three persons selected and appointed as follows: The city council of each of the said cities shall appoint one of the said revisors. .	.	. The Lieutenant Governor in Council shall appoint the other two revisors.
In Montreal these three gentlemen compose this hoard: the Hon. Justice F. X. Choquette, who is the president; Mr. George A. Morrison, K.C., and Mr. Harvey, K.C. In

January, they went over the list and found it correct, and the city council of Montreal is hound hy the law to send a copy of that list to Ottawa. This is the copy I have in my hand. The point I want to make is this: Is it necessary, when we have the guarantee of the reputation of Mr. Justice Choquette and of those other two gentlemen, that they will make up a proper list, that we should hand over the work to one enumerator who may be appointed to the dissatisfaction of the whole community? You are proposing to take the old list as a basil. Why could not Mr. Justice Choquette and the other two gentlemen add on the names of the women voters and strike out the names of foreigners whose names they think should be stricken out? Why put in this mushroom enumerator? The enumerator might be a kind of a dog mushroom, because there are different kinds of mushrooms. We shall have to watch the enumerator. I shall have to sit next to him in order to see that he does not strike out or add on names which should not be stricken out or added. By leaving the list to the Board of Revisors in Quebec and Montreal, there is every guarantee that it will be made up properly and to the satisfaction of all concerned. In that way also, the Government would save a great deal of money. In Quebec we have 65 counties, and there would' have to be at least 65 enumerators with the right of the returning officer of the county to name more; that is to say, one to every polling subdivision. I fail to understand why the Government is introducing this system of enumerators. We never had such a thing before in Quebec. Under subsection 62, a person may go to an enumerator and say: I have the right to vote. The enumerator may refuse, but he will generally give the right to vote to anybody so that it may be that in every booth there will be five or six or seven of those people coming to vote. What control have you in that case? The deputy returning officer or the representative of a candidate can challenge, but at the same time, if this person offers to swear, he must receive the vote. There will, therefore, be an electoral campaign in every polling booth. There will be discussion there as to whether such a person shall be allowed to vote or not. You will have one agent fighting against the other agent, and you will find that there is really no basis for the list. The list will apparently be made up, but at the same time it will be so disrupted by the enumerators that nobody will recognize it. There will be a fight in the booth. To save all this I would ask that
the Board of Revisors be permitted to revise the list in the city of Montreal, to receive all complaints, to strike out the names of foreigners whose names should be struck off and to add the names of the women whose names should, according to this measure, be added. You may take all the precautions you like to name a good enumerator, but he will be a partisan. Two years ago every one expected an election. The people of Montreal thought there would be an election.
Partisanship came in. I was asked to look after the revision of the electoral list of St. James, but I had no money to spend for that purpose. My opponent, however, had an office controlled by a great politician whom we sometimes see in this House. He appointed two men for each polling subdivision, and these two men made every one who applied to be put on the voters' list establish his qualifications. A man called Peter, we will say, would come along, and these two men would say, "We don't know Peter," and Peter would be struck off the list. About fifteen hundred names were struck off in that way. Last year 700 or 800 applied to be put on the voters' list in St James, and no organization was formed to strike off names. I thought the Government had possibly decided to prepare a new list. Pull opportunity was given to applicants to be put on the list. Does any cine expect that we will get justice if these enumerators are appointed? There is not the slightest doubt that the enumerators who will be appointed will be the best string-pullers in the municipality. They will be near to the Government in isome' way or other, and we shall have to look after our own interests. I think it would be far better to leave it to the judge.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
It is true that the enumerator makes a complete list and hands that list to the returning officer, but in making that list he is [DOT]compelled by law to put on every man who is on the list that exists for that poll, except aliens naturalized since March 31, 1902, and conscientious [DOT] objectors. He is also compelled to add the women who aTe enfranchised under this Bill, and those only. Those are his duties as defined by law. That work of his is subject to appeal to the judges. If Judge Choquette is the judge who would sit on a recount, he will sit and have just the same authority as before, and I hope he will exercise it well, as no doubt he will. Nothing else is subject to appeal. Why? Because it has all been judicially revised before.

We do not propose to appoint string-pullers or mushrooms as enumerators.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: These things might occur after the election.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
The election will not be decided until the judge is through with his work. As long as the result of the election depends upon his work, it makes no difference 'whether his work is done before or after polling day. It is the result that counts, and that result depends just as much upon the judicial work of the judge as if he did it before polling day. That is -the intent of the Act, and I am sure if my hon. friend will consult with his friends around him he will be advised that that is exactly what is embodied in the Bill.
My hon. friend from Carleton made a suggestion to us with regard to the boys who might from the date of the passing of this Act be enlisted for patrol work on the Canadian coast, and he asked that any so enlisted should not be counted among those whose female relatives would be permitted to vote. As soon as he made the proposal it struck me as reasonable, and he put it as a test of our sincerity.	I accept my
hon. friend's suggestion, and am prepared to embody it in the Bill. I do so for the reason that it is in line with the spirit of the Bill as it now stands. We declined to give the vote to the women relatives of the soldiers in Canada, and to my mind the chief reason was that it would admit of abuse. There would undoubtedly be the possibility of taking enlistments, and if there .is any possibility of that in connection with the naval forces around the shores of Canada I do not think it is unreasonable that the suggestion of my hon. friend should be accepted, and that 33A should be amended accordingly. Between six and eight o'clock I will prepare an amendment embodying the suggestion of my hon. friend.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: That i6 another reason.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
That is the principal
reason. Now the men in the patrol service around Canada are here and can exercise their influence to a much greater degree than the soldier who is in Canada, because the soldier is confined to. barracks and is not liable to get around among his neighbours, whereas the man in the patrol service is living at home, carrying on bis ordinary business, and just as much able to exercise his influence during an election as ever he was. in his lifetime. I do not think my hon. friend understands the conditions in the patrol service. These men are simply living at home and carrying on their ordinary occupations, and the Government is paying them for the boats. If there be any reason for excluding the women relatives of the soldier who is in Canada, there is a double reason for excluding the woman relatives of members of the patrol service. However I am very thankful for the small concession my hon. friend has made, and I hope he will take this further suggestion into consideration between now and eight o'clock.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
In connection with this
cloven-footed provision which disfranchises all British subjects who have been naturalized since March 31, 1902, I would like to ask the Secretary of State what evidence or proof, or what safeguard is there in this Bill as to the nature of the evidence that will be considered sufficient by the enumerator, or by the deputy returning officer, when a voter is voting and is challenged as to whether he was born in an alien enemy country.
Mr. MEIGHEN. The judge decides that.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: But here is a man who is making application vo the enumerator to go on the list, and he speaks the German language-

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: He is refused.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: But he was bom in the United States. The enumerator says: "Well, I don't know whether you were born in the United States or not." Is he refused by the enumerator?	.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: If he is bom dn the United States he should not be refused by the enumerator, and if he is refused he can vote and his vote will be counted.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: It will be tied up.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
But the enumerator
would not gain anything by that.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: How is the enumerator to decide whether this man should be put on the list? Ts he to take the man's word when he says that 'he was born in the United States, or that he was born in Germany? What proof must a man furnish? Surely, the Secretary of State does not expect a man to produce his birth certificate? It does not seem to me there is any safeguard here whatever.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: I think it would be unreasonable to demand a birth certificate if the man did not have if. If he had his birth certificate, of course he might be asked to produce it. I do not think there will be very much doubt as to the origin of the men who are under the jurisdiction of the enumerator, because he has only one poll and he knows the people. He has for years known what the public has generally considered was the place of birth of John Schmitz. He has understood it all along, and in the majority of cases it is clear there would be no dispute about it. If there was a dispute he could make inquiries from the neighbours, and so on, and if by any chance he was wrong, then dt comes before the judge, who takes such evidence us he would take in any civil proceedings. ,

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: When does it come before the judge?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: On the recount.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: It is tied up until then.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: But what is the difference? When this safeguard was put in, it was done in the belief that it secured absolute judicial revision, and for the life of me I cannot see why a judicial revision, which takes place before the result of the poll is determined, is not as effective as if there was no necessity at all for such revision.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
The safeguard spoken of by the Secretary of State does not seem to me to meet the point at all. The actual working-out of this feature will be this: if you get an active partisan as enumerator, and send him into a German-speaking polling division-a number of which I have in my own constituency-he can doubt any man's word, he can refuse to put the name of any German-speaking man on the list, and when that man comes to vote, his name
not being on the enumerator's list, if he votes at all he must swear in his vote. These votes will be put in envelopes, and will be considered before the judge on a recount. I can imagine in a constituency where there would be perhaps forty or fifty polling divisions, largely constituted of men of German birth or extraction, if the candidate wished to protect his interests and to protect the interests of every voter in those forty or fifty polling divisions, he might have to bring all these men before a judge on a recount to verify their right to vote.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: They have to swear to their exact qualification in order to vote.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: Exactly. It seems to me the scrutineer of that polling division might challenge every one of these votes, and compel the deputy returning officer to put them into envelopes to be brought before the judge in a recount.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: If the enumerator refuses to put a man's name on, and the man is prepared to' swear he has the right to vote, nobody can challenge that. It goes in the envelope anyway.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: So much the worse. If the man has to swear in order to vote, then automatically his vote goes into the envelope.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: If the enumerator makes him swear.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
Giving the enumerator
credit for being conscientious and trying to do the right thing, although a partisan, should we put upon him the responsibility of deciding as to whether or not a man who was born in the United States or in an alien enemy country, should or should not have the right to vote? I think that is an entirely unfair proposition.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: It is subject to judicial review.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: Supposing the man does swear in his vote, and he has to appear before the judge on recount. What evidence is the judge to accept?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
That position arises in every case. The judge will be governed by the laws of evidence. I do not know how you are going to determine anything ultimately except by the laws of evidence of this country. The rule of evidence is that the judge will demand the best evidence that can be secured. This would be-the certificate of birth, but if this certifi-

cate is not securable, then he gets the next best evidence that can be secured. That is plainly put in the rule of evidence, and that is the rale the judge will follow.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: I think it would be very much fairer to candidates and to voters if this Act were to state the class of evidence which would necessarily be accepted by the enumerator as to the place of a man's birth, so that if he were born in the United States, or in some friendly country, his name could be put on the list and he would not necessarily be sworn, and his vote tied up, nor would he be under the necessity of appearing before a judge on a recount.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: If that were done there would be the same difficulty.. If the enumerator is honest, he will take the best evidence he can get. If he is dishonest he will not. Supposing he is dishonest, and is told by the law to take such and such evidence, but does not do it, all the man can do is vote, and have his ballot tied. It would be tied anyway. As long as the man has his recourse to go before a judge of the land, no injustice can be done to him.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: The point I make is, that the enumerator has nothing in this Act to guide him as to what kind of proof or evidence is proof or evidence to him that the man is not entitled to be on the list?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: Nor has the judge anything to guide him under the ordinary law of the land. The judge has to take the best evidence available, and the enumerator has to do the same thing, and if you put up hard and fast rules I think hon. gentlemen will find the matter would be a .good deal worse than it is now.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: I see in the present arrangement the possibility of the entire vote of a polling division being tied up.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
The enumerator is not a
lawyer or a judge and he wants to know. I am assuming that he wants to be fair but there is the case of the man who does not want to be fair and who may say: If he tells, me that he is from the United States I am supposed to take his word. I would suggest that it would be a great injustice to ask a man in the short time of an election campaign to back up his claim to citizenship. The other man who is affected by this1 Act is a naturalized British subject and he has taken the oath of allegiance. He has a naturalization certificate. In taking his oath he gives his place of birth under circumstances that do not in any way tend to fraud. When he was taking out naturalization there was no reason why he should say that he was born in the United States when he was actually born in Germany. The naturalization certificate should be prima facie evidence as far as putting the man om the list is concerned. '

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: I too think it would be prima facie evidence but it would not be conclusive.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
That would miake it
conclusive.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
Suppose a man could
not find his affidavit and suppose also that his certificate was missing-we have provided that a judge can weigh the evidence of the man's right to vote without giving the absolute right to everybody who cannot locate his affidavit. He might have difficulty in getting his affidavit although he had his certificate.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: I want to call the minister's 'attention to clause 33(a). I take it that the female relatives, enumerated, of the man who has served overseas, whether he is back in this country or not, have the right to vote?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
In that case I would ask the Secretary of State to strike out the word " person " as it appears in line thirty of this clause:
Every female person shall be capable of voting and qualified to vote at a Dominion election in any province or in the Yukon Territory, who, being a British subject, and qualified as to age, race and residence as required in the case of a male person in such province or in the Yukon Territory, as the case may be, is the wife, widow, mother, sister or daughter of any person.
I would propose to insert "military elector" in place of "person."

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: And leave in "living or dead"?

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: Leave in the rest but substitute for "person" "military elector."

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: Then we would have to define "military elector."

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
That is defined in the Military Voters Act. I suggest that out of respect for the soldier himself. I was reading in the papers the other day about a man who was being chased around this country, an outlaw, who is a returned soldieT, a dynamiter named Monette or Girard. It is not right that the mother, wife, daughter or sister of a man who has been at the front and has served his country well should go to the poll with the wife or sister of this man Monette, an outlaw and a deserter, for whom the police have been looking. The term "military elector," although not contained in this Act, is defined in the .Military Voters Act, and I think that, for the honour and dignity of those men who are at the front and doing their duty, it is proper that it should be used in this Act Tather than the word "person." The definition of "military elector" in the Military Voters Act is:
"Military elector" means and includes every person, male or female, who, being a British subject, whether or not ordinarily resident in Canada and whether or not a minor or an Indian, has been, while within or without Canada, appointed, enlisted, enrolled or called out for active service as one of the Canadian Expeditionary Force, the Royal Canadian Navy, the Canadian Militia on active service, or the Royal Naval Canadian Volunteer Reserve, or has been, while within Canada, appointed, enlisted or enrolled as one of the British Royal Flying Corps, Royal Naval Aviation Service, or Auxiliary Motor Boat Patrol.
I have been looking over that clause, and f find that it covers every man whom the Minister of Naval Service would like to have included. It may extend the franchise a little farther than the Secretary of State intends.. We might restrict it, if the minister desires to do so, with reference to the men who have not yet left Canada. On the other hand, I would like the persons whose relatives are entitled to vote under clause 33 (a) to be designated as a "military elector" who is serving or who has been honourably discharged, instead of by the word "person."

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
The suggestion is a very valuable one. It did not occur to me that the relatives of a deserter would be included here, hut I rather think they would be. It would be quite wro-ng that the relatives of
those who had joined and deserted should be on a par with the relatives of the man who was serving or who had been honourably discharged.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
Section 63 of the Act
as it new stands provides that any person, practically, who is on the voters' list can be challenged and if he refuses to take the oath in form Z he cannot vote. Then section 65 provides that every voter shall be entitled to vote whose name is on the voters' list and has not been erased therefrom in accordance with the foregoing provisions of this Bill. I assume that the enumerator takes the list as it comes from the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery or the custodian of the list in New Brunswick, erases from it the names of any former alien enemies, and adds the names of the female voters, and that becomes the list for the election. Therefore it- seems that every voter is entitled to vote whose name is on. the list unless he refuses to take the oath in form Z. But form Z merely refers to people in Saskatchewan, Alberta and the Yukon Territory and not in the rest of Canada. At section 153 it will he found that in the rest of Canada we have a distinct cause of challenge on the ground that a man does not comply with the qualification provided by the provincial statute. In New Brunswick, he must take an oath that he is a resident of the constituency in which he attempts to vote; but if you leave the Bill as it is now, you lender nugatory that provision of our law which prevents him from voting in a constituency in which he does not reside. In other words, it comes back to what I said earlier in the afternoon; in my. constituency, I have no doubt there are from 100 to 200 names on the voters' lists who do not live in the constituency and have not for years, but who, for political reasons, have been deliberately kept on those lists in order that they may be brought from the United States to vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: How can they vote? 'hey have to take the oath, and that would be perjury.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
They do. But there has been a change in the East and the man who attempts to perjure himself now will be in the worst scrape he ever was in. It will be no longer safe for a man to come from Boston or the state of Maine and perjure himself because his name is on the voters' list. But if the law stands as it is now I am afraid that man will be safe and we cannot put the oath to him because,

once his name is on the list, he oan come from Boston or anywhere and we cannot prevent him because, being on the list made out by an enumerator, he has a right to vote. That means a serious thing to me, perhaps 100 or 150 votes. I would ask the minister to look into this carefully before eight o'clock.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess.
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
Before the Secretary of State replies to the question that I put to him before six o'clock, I should like to call his attention to the provisions of section
63 of the Act as it now stands. The section reads:
Every person whose name is on the voters' list, unless sworn as in the next preceding section provided, shall before being permitted to vote, if required by any candidate, agent or elector, take the oath number one in Form Z.
If he refuses to take the oath, his name shall be erased from the voters' list. But the swearing " in the next preceding section provided " is that in the case of persons who have been addled to the list by the certificate of the enumerator on election day. Section 62 provides challenge only for a limited number of people; section 63 is the general 'Challenge provision, hut my hon. friend will find that form Z could not be used at all except in Saskatchewan, Alberta, and the Yukon territory.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
Form Z is omitted. Section 62, page 8 of the Bill, says:
(q) by striking out Form Z No. 1 and inserting instead the following:
"Form Z No. 1. You swear that you are legally qualified to vote at this election, that you are of the ('male' or 'female') sex, a British subject, and of the full age of 21 years.''
I had this matter looked into during the recess, and those who looked into it are thoroughly' satisfied-from their report to me I think that they are right-that that fully meets the point raised by the hon. gentleman before six o'clock. The amendment to form Z makes form Z the proper oath to be taken by all persons other than those who are sworn because the enumerator will not let them go on the list.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
Legally the minister is right, but that is not sufficient for my purpose. Section 153 of the Dominion Elections Act, which was added in 1909, before the last general election, at the request of members from New Brunswick, was de-

signed to meet the very condition I have pointed out1 to the minister. We have had a terrible condition of affairs in New Brunswick because of the fact that the names of men who live in the United States have been kept on the lists. They are brought into the province for a consideration amounting anywhere from $5 to $25, and in some cases $50. My hon. friend (Mr. Graham) says, "pretty high." I can tell him that they have paid as high as $100- as a matter of fact, $100 was a kind of upset price against me in 1911. These men were brought - over and swore that they were qualified. In order to meet that condition section 153 was inserted, providing that, in addition to complying with the general law, a man must take any oath provided for by provincial legislation. There is an oath in the law of New Brunswick in which a man must specifically swear that lie is a resident of the electoral district in which he is tendering his vote.
I do object, therefore, to seeing this provision cut out when it might as well be " left in.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
It is still there, and can be used. Section 153 will lose none of its force in the coming election by virtue of this Act. It says:
Except in the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta and the Yukon Territory, an elector, if required by the deputy returning officer, the poll clerk, one of the candidates, or an agent of a candidate, or by any elector present, shall, before receiving his ballot paper, take' such oath of qualification as by the laws of the province he may in the like case at a provincial election be required to take, such changes having been made in the form of oath as are necessary to make it applicable to the election being held.
Make it applicable to this election, and the man is bound to be qualified by residence in order that he may be enabled to vote. The hon. gentleman can make up an affidavit in accordance with that, and if the man refuses to take it he cannot vote.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: I cannot make up an affidavit. All any person can do is to ask the man to take the oath provided by law.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: By the provincial law.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: Is section 153 allowed to stand?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
My hon. friend does
not specifically repeal it, but he does so in effect by the provisions of section 65 of this Act. Section 65 says:	.

Every voter shall be entitled to vote whose name is on the voters' list and has not been erased therefrom in accordance with the foregoing provisions of this part.
We could demand that a man take the vote according to the new form Z, but that is not sufficient. A person who, for a consideration, comes to the poll with the avowed purpose of voting when he knows he has no right to do so, asserts that he is qualified to vote. If you make him swear that he is a resident of the electoral district in which he tenders his vote, then you can get after him with a warrant five minutes afterwards. That is what we want him to swear, and that is why section 153 was put in. That provision has been useful to us. I suggest that section 153 should read this way:
Every voter shall be entitled to vote whose name is on the voters' list and has not been erased therefrom in accordance with the foregoing provisions of this Part, and subject to the provisions of section 153.
Just add those words. Then you will retain the rights given us by section 153.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: The rights are still retained even if you do not do that. The hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) is not in agreement with my hon. friend.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: I think the hon. member for South Renfrew and I are entirely in agreement in regard to the matter.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: Does the hon. member say that, if at the end of section 65, you make section 153 the dominating section, then in Ontario a man who is on the list, say in the county of Renfrew, and who has moved into the county of Leeds, a sufficiently long time to disqualify him in the county of Renfrew, could, under the provincial law, still vote in the county of Renfrew? I am afraid he could not.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: I do not think he could. The hon. member for Carleton and I had a little conversation. The point I had in mind was this. I was anxious to have some oath that the man who is on the list confirmed by this measure could be asked to take as to his right to vote. He may have got on the voters' list without having any right to get on.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: When he got on?

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
Yes. He may have got on wrongly. I see the difficulty the Secretary of State is'in. By accepting this provision, as he says, a man who had moved out of the county would be prevented from
coming back and voting, and consequently he would have no vote. Would it meet the purposes of my hon. friend from Carleton if the man had to swear that he was a resident of the province?

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: No.	.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: That is the difficulty.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: It would hardly be fair to say, so far as Ontario is concerned, that a man should have to swear he was a resident of that riding, because provision is made in this Bill that a man having removed from the riding and, I suppose, being still in Canada-*

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: -should have a right to' return. If not, he would not have a right to vote in this election.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: That is it exactly.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
I have another suggestion to make, which will not interfere with the condition of affairs in Ontario. We have, in a dozen places in this measure, made certain provision respecting one, two or three provinces. Therefore, we are not violating any principle if we make a special provision for a special province. I would suggest that section 65 read:
Every voter shall be entitled to vote whose name is on the voters' list and has not been erased therefrom in accordance with the foregoing provisions of this Part and in the province of New Brunswick subject to the provisions of section 153.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: I find it very hard to agree with that, for the reason that the cases of the two provinces are identical.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: I may be in error in that. This is the law in our province: If a man's name is upon the list, say, in the county of Carleton, and he moves to the city of St. John just before an election, he must vote in the constituency in which he resides. All he has to do is to apply to the secretary-treasurer who is the custodian of the list in the county of Carleton and obtain from him a certificate which he takes to the secretary-treasurer of the city of St. John, and this entitles him to vote in the city of St. John. That is the way in which we work it out.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
Is there no time limit
fixed?

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: No.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: Would that be the case even if the man went the day before an election?

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: If he became a bona fide resident of the city of St. John the day .before the election and became a qualified voter under the authority of that certificate, he would ,be entitled to vote.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: The case is not the same in Ontario.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: That is the difference.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
A good many people
have moved into New Brunswick just a few days before election. What I have stated is the law, so that you do not deprive the man of his vote by .applying .section 153 to him. He has the right to take his vote with him.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: Not under this law.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
No, under our law he
ihas the right to take his vote with him. I feel, therefore, that some provision should be made .by which we can retain the provisions of section 153.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
By enumerators? The
Lord forbid!

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
You could call them
registrars. If the hon. gentleman wants seventy-five per cent of the list completed now and final, I think it has to stay that way. I do not see how we can invade the list and, at the same time, preserve the principle at .all.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
That is exactly the point
we were discussing last night. I think the principle ought to be accepted that a citizen of Canada who is qualified to vote should not, be disqualified because he has moved from one part of the country to an-

other. We have adopted the principle that there should be one vote for each man. The provisions in New Brunswick, .as the hon. member for Carleton has stated, cover that point to a certain extent-but I do not think as fairly as they should-to allow that man to return and vote in the constituency in which he was. on the list provided that he was not on the list in any other part of the country. It does not seem to be right that any citizen of this country who has voting qualifications, if by reason of business necessity or otherwise he has moved into another part and has not been in that.district a sufficient length of time to be on the list, should be in the position of an 'alien and entirely disfranchised. Provided that a man is on the list only in one constituency and has been continuously resident in this country and is qualified in one cons tituency, he cannot have been away very long, and I do not see why he should be deprived of bis vote. So far as justice to the voter is concerned, it would give precisely the same conditions as exist in New Brunswick except that the voter would return to' the place in which he was on the list instead of voting in the place in which he resides.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: I do not think he would have a vote there at all under Form Z.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: That would not apply, I suppose, in the province of Quebec, because no man can be added to the list according to 65 A.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: No, it only applies to women.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: The objection of the hon. member for Carleton, as I understand it. is that men not resident in Canada at all may come in and vote. I think we could shut out the vote that might be brought in from across the line by adding to Form 7, No. 1, after the word "British subject" the words "a resident of Canada."

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: I am inclined to think that that could be done, if it will suit the needs of the hon. member for Carleton.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: It will get rid of most of the difficulty. Let me give an illustration. In our country we have many cases where a man may be revised in two counties. Perhaps he has land in both counties, and he goes on the assessment list. Of course, he should be removed from the county in which he does not reside. He might attempt to vote twice, but that is a local affair, and it is watched pretty closely. If my hon. friend would insert the words "a resident of Canada" I think it would about meet the case.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: I beg to move that Form 7 No. 1 be amended by adding after the word "subject" in the third line thereof the words "a resident of Canada."

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
I move:
That section 1 of the Bill be amended by striking out of the fourth line of the amended section 48, paragraph (i) of the Bill, the word "ten" and substituting therefor the word "fifteen."
This is to make the period between {'he posting up and the election day fifteen days instead of ten.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: Referring to Form Z No. 1. sometimes difficulty arises in connection with the interpretation of what is meant by " a resident of Canada". I think it should be understood that a man is held to be domiciled 'where his family resides.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.

speechtext: No.
