speechtext: Will the Secretary of State permit me a word in connection with the opening of the poll? Section 136 of some Bill I have in hand-and it is very difficult to tell what we axe working on-deals with certain cities, the cities of Calgary, Edmonton, Halifax, Hamilton, London, Montreal, Ottawa, Quebec, Regina, St. John, Toronto, Vancouver, Victoria and Winnipeg wherein the polls shall be open at the hour of six o'clock in the morning. As I may not be present when this section comes up for discussion, I would like to say that the city of Stratford, in the constituency of North Perth, which I have the honour to represent, is a large railway centre, and the early trains leave that city eviery morning except Sunday long before the usual hour for'the opening of the polls. These trains leave for Buffalo, Port Dover, Toronto Montreal, Owen Sound, London, Detroit, Sarnia, main line to Chicago, and Goderich division and on only one of these divisions is it possible for the train crews to poll their votes. I (think the city of Stratford should be included in this list, as it is one of the largest railway centres in the province of Ontario.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
This is a question on which I think the committee should be guided largely by the views of the members who know most about the cities. If it is in the public interest in any city that the polls should open at six o'clock instead of at nine o'clock, we want the Bill to read that they shall open at six o'clock. I may say I have also been requested to add the city of St. Thomas to the list. I think it would be a great advantage to the committee if horn, members would carefully review the ground, and let the committee have the benefit of their ideas as to how the section should be amended, if it needs amendment at all. There is ho reason why the city of Stratford should not be added to the list if it is going to be a public convenience.

At the same time we do not want to impose on cities that do not need it the necessity of opening the poll at six o'clock in the morning.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: I think nearly all divisional points on the railways would be in the same position.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: I would like to have an expression from the Secretary of State to the effect that no matter what other members of the House will say or do, he will put Stratford in the Bill.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: I am quite ready to do so.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
At the opening of the session this afternoon, I asked the Secretary of State if since last evening he had taken into consideration the enfranchisement of relatives of persons serving in the Canadian navy within Canada. He informed me it was not the intention to limit the enfranchisement to those without Canada. At the time I was not sure whether I should be in order in pressing my point, and I abandoned it for the time being. Now, however the discussion is quite free and open, and I wish again to direct attention to this matter. I do not think it is wise or necessary to enfranchise the female relatives of those serving in the Canadian navy within Canada. I understand this Bill is based upon the principle that we have a great number of men serving abroad in France and elsewhere in Europe; many of them on account of death of course will not be able to vote. In introducing this Bill, the Secretary of State expressed the view that it would be but proper if some of the relatives of those deceased soldiers should have the right to vote.
He urged as another justification for the Bill the fact that the influence of the soldiers was lost. They had an opportunity of voting but they had not an opportunity of exercising any influence during the campaign in Canada. That is another of the two grounds upon which he justified this Bill when introducing it. That ground does not apply to the naval forces. Surely within Canada the relatives of this class ought not to be given the franchise. They have an opportunity of exercising their influence in Canada, and I cannot understand upon what principle my hon. friend desires to enfranchise the female relatives of these men. I submit that it should not be done. According to the statement read to the committee this afternoon by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, it includes some

classes of people who, in the strict sense of the term, are not engaged in the naval service. In that statement the minister says:
It would also include the relatives of men employed in clerical positions in Ottawa, Halifax or elsewhere who never sailed in a ship and are employed continually ashore.
I submit that it is not fair to extend the franchise to the female relatives of men employed in the dock yards at Halifax or in tlte naval service department here at Ottawa. Proceeding further the statement says:
It would also include the relatives of officers serving in Canada on Imperial duty such as the officers of the Naval Patrol in Halifax, the staff in charge of the dispatch of convoys at Sydney,
And so on. There is no particular reason why the relatives of this class should he enfranchised. I find, according to the statement, that on the east coast of Canada there are 149 boys and on the west coast 53. Their female relatives will be enfranchised. If the minister would apply the principles upon which he justified the Bill itself, to this part of the Bill referring to the naval service, he would strike out the words "within or" at the bottom of the first page. The female relatives of men serving in the military forces of Canada, and within Canada, are not enfranchised; why should the relatives of those engaged in the naval service in Canada be enfranchised? Why not apply the same principle to both the military and naval forces? I understood last evening that the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State were rather disposed to, view this application of mine favourably. No reason was given this afternoon in justification of this particular section. I hope the minister will see his way clear to restrict the application of this clause.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: I regret that I am not able to agree with the hon. the junior member for Halifax and I am a little surprised that an hon. gentleman who favours the extension of the franchise to all women should wish to restrict it in this way. I should think that if he were in favour of universal suffrage he would be glad to have it extended as far as possible and that if he could not get the whole loaf he would want the half loaf to be as large as possible.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
I cannot follow
that line of reasoning.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
I am sorry if the hon. gentleman cannot follow my argument. There is a great distinction as far as the
peril and danger is concerned between the soldiers doing garrison duty, or training in Canada, and the sailors on a ship along our coast. I think there could be no more dangerous avocation than that followed by those brave men who to-day are protecting the shores and coasts of eastern Canada. They are watching out for mines, they are continually menaced by the danger of striking an unknown mine, of being torpedoed, of running into a hostile ship, and the dangers of the sea. There is no more hazardous occupation than that which is followed by the brave men to whom I desire to tender this well-deserved tribute. I believe the anguish that is suffered by the relatives of those brave men is almost as great as that which is endured by the women relatives of those who are at the front.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: Where does this anguish come in? What is the cause of all this anguish on the part of the relatives of men employed on. some ships in Halifax who only do about two hours' work a day?

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
I am afraid that my
hon. friend is hard of heart.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: No, he is not at all. Tell me where this anguish comes from.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
Any good woman,
when her .husband is exposed to danger on the sea, naturally suffers anguish, and these men who go out even for two hours on the Atlantic coast brave the danger of submarines, hostile craft and inclement weather. They are in a most dangerous position. The suffering and anguish of their female relatives is akin to that suffered by the female relatives of men at the front.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
My hon. friend
must be thinking of phantom ships of the enemy or " ships that pass in the night." Surely he is not talking about real ships of the enemy that are a menace to these Canadian ships of ours?

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
I am surprised that
my hon. friend would' refer to the Canadian navy as a phantom. I am astounded at the hon. gentleman contending that there are no dangers on the ocean these days. It is full of dangers and there could be no more hazardous occupation than that which is followed by these men. From the standpoint of suffering for the cause and for the flag, we are abundantly justified in giving the brave women relatives of these sailors the privilege of the franchise and
57.3t

I sincerely trust that it *will not be denied them by this statute.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: This Bill will enfranchise the female relatives of 57 wireless operators on the Atlantic coast and So on the West coast. Does my hon. friend mean to tell me that the wives and sisters and mothers of these men employed as wireless operators have to undergo anguish? Are these wireless operators exposed to great dangers and menaces of any kind?

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: I say emphatically that wireless operators are exposed to danger. And I would ask my hon. friend if there are no mines along the Atlantic coast, if there is no danger from that source, what in the world are these men doing cruising and searching for them?

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: They are not doing much of it.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: But every day they are out.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: Once in a while.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: I happen to know thiat they are out.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: I should like to hear from the Secretary of State as to my suggestion to amend this Bill. The hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Davidson) is subject to some hallucination about this matter. The protection of our coast is really performed by the ships of the British Navy which are stationed upon the coast. There are a great number of small steamers in the harbour of Halifax whose officers and crews, I believe, come within this Bill-three or four times more than are necessary; half of them might be dispensed with entirely. They are exposed to no such dangers as my hon. friend would have this committee believe.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: It might rain on them.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: When this Bill was presented to the House by the Solicitor General, he laid stress on the fact that it gave the franchise to the female relatives of overseas soldiers who, by reason of their absence, were unable to exercise any influence in the coming election in this country. I can understand this ground, although I do not believe 'in it; but why should it apply to men to the navy?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
I believe in both
grounds and therefore support the Bill; but I cannot understand the hon. member who says he does not believe in these grounds
[Mr. Davidson. J
at all and still does not want the line pressed one inch beyond them. I am willing to concede that the ground of absence and consequent loss of influence among the electorate is eliminated in the case of those who spend a considerable part of their time on shore with their fellows; but the other ground of sacrifice, the exposure of husbands or sons to the perils of war, applies to those whose husbands and sons are serving in the navy for the protection of our coast. If that is not so, let us say that the whole coast defence is a fake, and that the whole idea of a Canadian navy for coast defence is a fraud. I do not think the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) would want to take that ground. I never contended that there was not need for coast defence even in peace, and I believe that to-day there is need 9 p.m. for every kind of coast defence.
I also believe that those engaged in it are exposed to the same perils in mine-sweeping and so on as in any other form of service.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
Where is the
mine-sweeping being done in Canada?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
The Minister of Marine told us this afternoon where it was done.
Mr. A. K. MACLEAN- I do not believe there is any mine sweeping outside of the harbours of Sydney and Halifax, and possibly in the river St. Lawrence.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: I have to take my information from the Department of Marine. The minister said that extensive minesweeping operations were going on in connection with the coast patrol.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: There may be some patrolling, but no such thing as minesweeping on the coast.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: That is dangerous.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: No, it is not.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
Before six o'clock I was suggesting an amendment to the Solicitor General in the definition of persons who could give a right to vote to their female relatives. The Solicitor General raised an objection that would disappear if he yielded to the demand of the hon. member for Halifax. I suggested the use of the words "military elector" in place of the word "person." He objected that the word military elector might includ& people in camp in Canada who had never been overseas. The clause already provides for that in respect to1 the military forces. The soldier who has not gone across the seas cannot

give the vote to his female relations. If a similar clause were inserted in relation to the naval force, everything would be all right. I do not see why a difference should be made between the man who serves in the navy and the man who serves in the land forces.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: I think my hon. friend's suggestion had far more value than he attributes to it. His suggestion was to substitute for "person" in 33a "military elector" on the first page of the amending Act, limiting "military elector to those who had not left the Canadian shores. The great value of the suggestion was that as the Act stands, a man who enlisted and deserted perhaps a week afterwards is placed in the same position as a man who is still fighting in Flanders; his relatives [DOT]have the right to vote just as do the relatives of the bona fide soldier. My hon. friend suggests that that class of relatives should not be enfranchised; certainly they should not be. I propose to meet my hon. friend fully on that point. Indeed, I am obliged to him for the 'suggestion, because it is wrong that the relatives of a deserter should be given the vote under any principle embodied in this Bill.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: How does my hon. friend differentiate between the man serving in the military and land forces and the man serving in the naval forces? As I understand it, the moment a man in the naval forces goes outside the three-mile limit he has gone overseas for the purpose of service.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: You could never tell whether a man was just outside the three-mile limit or not.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: "Without 'Canada" are the words used in the Act.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
"Without Canada"
legally means beyond the thTee-mile limit. Actual war service is frequently performed by members of the naval forces within the three-mile limit along the Canadian coast. T'he war service of a man in the military forces is not so performed; his active service is performed overseas. That is the difference. The men who are guarding the Canadian coasts are engaged in war service. It is conceivable that that service may become even more perilous than service overseas.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
Does the Secretary of State justify the enfranchisement of female relatives of those engaged in the
naval service upon the ground that the latter are subjected to peril?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: That they are engaged in actual war service involving peril.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: I suppose some of them are engaged in war service, but in many instances it is almost a commercial transaction. For instance, there are 92 wireless operators in the naval service of Canada. Does the work of a wireless operator constitute war service in the strictest sense of the term? Is that not a purely commercial occupation?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: I do not think they are in the naval service.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: They are in the naval service, according to the statement made this' afternoon by the Minister of the Naval Service. In Halifax harbour probably a dozen motor boats and steamers are operated by the Government, whereas three or four, or at least half the number, would be sufficient.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: What are they doing?

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: Some of them do nothing. A good many of them hardly ever go outside the mouth of the harbour. Some of them are engaged in the mine-sweeping in the harbour which is not a hazardous occupation.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: They are practising minesweeping.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: They are under instructions from the British Admiralty to sweep Halifax harbour for mines every day. They may be practising, but I suppose that work has to be done in any case. In many instances, these 'steamers have been chartered from individuals. In taking over the steamers, the Government took over the crew; automatically, I suppose, the men entered the naval service. Surely my hon. friend cannot justify the extension of the franchise to the female relatives of these men on the ground that they are subjected to peril or that they are actually engaged in war service.	.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: I suppose the hon. gentleman would take the same position in regard to the men engaged in forestry work in France. There is a minimum of peril there, I should think. You cannot distinguish between one war service and another.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
Is it not a fact that about a year ago a number of men were lost off



the patrol boat Grilse? These are the men whom he speaks of as not being engaged in perilous service.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: It is true that the Grilse on her way from Halifax to Bermuda met with disaster and some lives were lost. That steamer should not have been sent to sea at the time.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: The same thing is liable to occur to any one of the boats in this patrol service.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: She was the largest boat on the east coast engaged in patrol service. The case of the Grilse is evidence of the fact that the greater part of the patrol service down there is unnecessary. The Grilse never performed any large amount of service while there; she never should have been sent there. She is capable of real service, not on the Canadian coast but on the coast of the United Kingdom, on account of her great speed.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
knows that this patrol service extends far beyond Newfoundland. Several Newfoundland harbours are patrolled in the same way.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: I do not know it, and I doubt very much whether my hon. friend does.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
We are informing the
hon. gentleman now of the facts.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: Who is informing me?

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
You cannot tell what
moment a submarine will arrive off the coast of Nova Scotia and blow up one of the fishing towns.	,

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
I do not accept my hon. friend as an authority on this matter. Men much more familiar with matters'of this kind than the Secretary of State, the member for North Simeoe (Mr. Currie) or myself, say that the patrol service on the Atlantic coast is largely unnecessary-and I believe that is a fact. I should like the minister to give the commute some reason for retaining in the Bill as it now stands the clause to which I refer. Is it not peculiar that the female relatives of wireless operators should be enfranchised? A great number of men in this service in the city of Halifax never go to sea. Possibly there may be grounds of extending the -franchise to some female relatives in some cases, but it is unnecessary and unfair to leave the provision so-

broad and so unrestricted as it is in its present form.
Mr. MEIGHEN. It is putting me at an unfair advantage to ask me to defend the Naval Department and to proceed on the assumption that the Naval' Department is making a fraud of its work. I am not the Minister of Naval Service, but I am satisfied that the hon. gentleman's allegations in that regard are not founded upon fact. Wireless operators surely go out to sea. I assume that the mine-sweepers have wireless operators on board

men who are enlisted in the naval forces. What is the difference between a man who is a wireless operator on a mine-sweeper and a man who is a paymaster of a -battalion? There are degrees of peril, degrees of service, degrees of hard work, endurance, suffering. You cannot draw an exact line in that respect.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: Quite a number of wireless operators perform service on land.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: I assume they are sometimes on land and sometimes on ship. Take the men engaged in construction and forestry work; some of them are working in England; some of them may at no time be in France. The only bold line you can draw-the fairest line, without going into details in individual cases-is the lihe between active war service and something there is not war service of any kind. Mr. DAVIDSON': My hon. friend from Halifax (Mr.*A. K. Maclean) takes altogether too complacent a view of the marine situation in this country. I am surprised that my hon. friend, who has so long represented a marine constituency, does not appreciate the very great danger that besets the men that go down to the sea in ships, particularly warships, even in time of peace. If he will allow his memory to go back only a few years, he will remember that the Canadian warship, the Niobe, when the sky was clear, when there was no war, went down to attend a social function at Yarmouth during Home Week. There were no submarines, no mines, nothing of that kind. Yet that gallant ship came to grief even in time of peace. How very different those times are from now. We know that submarines have visited this side of the Atlantic-and not phantom submarines, by any means. Was it a phantom submarine that arrived off Nantucket a few months ago and sank a number of British ships? I think not. It is an open secret to all who live along the Nova Scotia coast that there is a great menace arising in that way. subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
I think I have discovered a solution for all these difficulties. There are two- classes in Canada who are away from home a great deal. The men of one class never know when they are going to be home, and the other class may know that they are going to be home for week-end; I refer to railroad [DOT]men and commercial travellers. In this Bill there is a clause providing for the opening of the polls in certain cities within municipalities at 6 a.m. This is ostensibly for the purpose of allowing railroad men and commercial travellers, and any others who may so desire, to vote early in the morning, it being presumed that commercial travellers and railroad men will be leaving home early in the .morning. This provision will .be of some benefit, no doubt, but as regards railway men it does not begin to meet their case. Every person who has lived in a railway centre, large or small, knows that railway men are liable to be called out at any hour of the day or night. It has very frequently occurred in my experience that crews have been called out at 'ten or eleven, or early in the morning, and they would be away from home long before six o'clock, and their runs would not alow them to return in time to cast their vote. The same thing might be said with regard to commercial travellers, though perhaps not to the same extent, because some commercial travellers at least can get home for polling day, but those who have a large territory to cover cannot do it. In the province of Saskatchewan special provision has been made for taking the vote of railway men and commercial travellers. In some of the states of the Union it is provided that an elector can vote wherever he is. He is not deprived of his vote by travelling, no matter how far away he may be from his own constituency. I would not suggest that we go as far as that, but would urge the Secretary

of State, now that we are dealing with this matter, to avoid the necessity of naming city after city, and town after town-as will have to be the case, and as is the case-by providing a clause similar to that in the Saskatchewan Act which would be applicable to every terminal point of a railway. That would cover the railway men's vote at any rate. The Saskatchewan Act strikes me as being very simple, and I think it is surrounded with all the necessary safeguards. If the committee will permit me, I will read one or two sections from their Act. Section 286 reads as follows:
Section 287 to 295 inclusive of this Act shall apply only to railway employees, commercial travellers and other persons whose employment or calling is such as to necessitate from time to time their absence from their places of residence, who are qualified electors under this Act in the electoral divisions or portions of electoral divisions mentioned in form 57 in the schedule to this Act, and who have reason to believe that they will be absent from their places of residence on the day fixed by the writ for the election.
2S7. For the purpose of enabling every such person to vote at any election held in the said electoral divisions the returning officer shall establish a special polling place in the city or town mentioned in form 57 in the schedule hereto as forming the whole or part of such division, which polling place shall be centrally located so as to suit the convenience of the voters.
The next -section gives the method by which the vote is to be taken. Then section 289 reads:
The poll at each such polling place so established shall be open between the hours of seven and ten o'clock in the afternoon on the three days exclusive of Sunday immediately preceding the day of election.
That is, the poll is open from seven to ten in the evening for three days previous to polling day, so that all the railway men and commercial travellers may register their votes on one of those three preceding days. Every night the ballot boxes are sealed, just as is done in an ordinary election. The ballots are perfectly safe, and are not counted until the end of the proper polling day. That seems to me to be a pretty simple provision, which I think could well be worked into this Act. Any one who has had anything to do with elections in a railway centre has felt the necessity for some better provision than we have ever jhad for allowing the railway men to vote. It is not the fault of the railway men if they are ordered out and must go. "First in, first out"; if it is their turn to go, they cannot remain. A provision such as is in the Saskatchewan Act would remove all possibility of manipulation. For instance,
the superintendent, or the man at the head of a railway company, who is friendly to one candidate has it in his power to order out the crews who do not agree with his views, and keep the men in who do agree with his views. There has been a good deal of complaint about that, and it is not fair to the men themselves. The railway men, who take a very deep interest in public affairs are very often unable to cast their votes, and I think it would only be doing justice to these men to have a provision in this Act such as I have -mentioned.
The same thing might be said with regard to commercial travellers. When a member of the Government I was waited' on by both these bodies on several occasions, and urged to devise means whereby they could vote. I suggested several-methods, but the men handling the justice end of the Government did not see it my way. I have observed that the Saskatchewan Act meets in a large measure what F have in mind, and if the minister could adopt something of that kind it would cover, the case and meet the wishes of the railway men, commercial travellers, and others of. that class, and also the wishes of tnose for whofn the hon. member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy) has spoken.

The hon. gentleman said just now that the law provided that the employer of labour should give the man an hour for voting. Take the city of Three Rivers, for instance, which is a city of about 20,000 or 22,000 inhabitants. They give the men an hour extra at noon to vote, and the result is there is such a congestion at the polling booths that the men cannot vote,

because it is not only the workingmen who are trying to vote, but business men who are going up to lunch will stop at the polling tooths also. I have seen cases where a good many men could not vote within the hour allowed them by the employers because there was too much congestion. It is well to open the poll early in the morning in order to give the railway men and the commercial travellers a chance to vote, but if we are to choose between the two classes, the workingmen and the railway men or travellers, I would take the workingmen, because they are more numerous. I do not suppose there would be more than one commercial traveller in 100 or 200 votes. More will suffer proportionately if you close the poll at five o'clock in the evening than if you open it late in the morning. If you open the poll early and close it late, it may be said that it would be too hard on the deputy returning officers, or on the clerks; but I do not think that is a very serious matter. If you open the poll at six o'clock in the morning and close it at seven or eight o'clock in the evening, you would give the. labouring man the advantage of being able to vote if he could not do it during the hour granted him by his employer for that purpose.

speechtext:
I am surprised to see so many hon. gentlemen on the other side have become quite familiar with Hull only recently. They will bear me out in saying that we have the E. B. Eddy Company, the Matthews-Laing Company, the Gilmour-Hughson Company, and several other manufacturing companies of considerable importance. The voters in the city of Hull

would have really little time to vote between twelve and one o'clock. The difficulty suggested by my hon. friend from Three Rivers applies with great force to the city of Hull, and I would like to see the Secretary of State insert a clause in the Bill that manufacturers in cities of over 18,000 population shall give their employees two hours instead of one for lunch on polling day.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: The question brought to the attention of the House by my hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) in connection with the Franchise Act of Saskatchewan, is one which seems to me to be worthy of consideration, and I speak with some understanding of the wants of the commercial traveller, because I had the honour of being a director of the Western Ontario Commercial Travellers for some years. The inconveniences and difficulties surrounding the polling of the commercial travellers' vote are generally known in the commercial districts. The principle of having Monday as a polling day for the commercial traveller has not met with the requirements of the commercial travellers. In the city of London, and I think in the city of Toronto and some other cities, in municipal elections, they have the polling on Monday invariably, but this has not resulted in polling a large commercial travellers' vote. A great many of these commercial travellers are out for two or three weeks at a time. I agree with the idea suggested by the hon. member for South Renfrew, that it might be practicable to get this class of men if arrangements could be made for taking the commercial travellers' vote on the Thursday, Friday and Saturday preceding the day of election. Because, if an election comes on Thursday and you arrange to open the poll on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday, the advantage to the commercial traveller is practically nil, for the reason that he goes out on Monday and will be out for the whole week, and cannot, without great expense to his firm and inconvenience to himself and his business, arrange to get in and poll his vote. This question is not a new one. It has been before the House in connection with the different Election Acts which have been passed.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: Do I understand my hon. friend to say that Friday is a better day than Monday for the commercial travellers-to poll their votes?

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
No, my hon. -friend did not understand me correctly. I tsay at certain

hours on Thursday, Friday 'and Saturday previous to |the election. In the great majority of cases commercial men are at home from Friday night to Monday morning. Some of them are at home on Thursday. I do not mean to keep the poll open the whole time, hut if it were open for, eay, three hours at the end of the week it would meet the requirements, whereas if it were open on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday during the week and the election was held on Thursday, it would not meet the requirements because the men would be out on the road. My hon. friend has also said that if special consideration is to be given to any vote it ought to be given to the labour vote because that is the larger vote.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
I said that if something
had to be sacrificed it should be sacrificed to .the more numerous element.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
I agree with my hon friend that the labour vote is a larger vote and that it ought to have facilities extended to it by giving workingmen a certain time to vote during the day. We had this question up in 1914 and it was discussed fully then. I brought to the attention of the House at that time the fact that there were employers whose political prejudices were so strong that they put obstacles in the way of their men going out to vote. They -would say:	Of course, you have the right
to go and vote; if you want to exercise the right that is given to you by the law, do it, but you will understand what the consequences will be. I believe that there 'should be hours -arranged for the workingmen to go *and vote. The Bill should specifically provide that there should be two or two and a half hours in the day when every employee of. a factory should have the right to vote or, if necessary, there should be alternative hours during which some of the employees, if all could not go at one time, should be allowed to go and vote. The Act should not make it permissive, but it should be m^de obligatory on the part of the employer to permit his employees to poll their votes without reference to the political prejudices of the employer.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
I do not object to having the polls open at -six in the morning for the accommodation of the railway men, but I think this matter can be dealt with in another way. The labour men have been asking that election day shall be declared to be a legal holiday. If we had a legal holiday on the day that the general election is held it would obviate the necessity of

making provision to meet a great many of the suggestions which have been brought before the committee to-night. While the polls will have to be opened at six in the morning for the railway men, it would not . be necessary with reference tO' any other business, because the men would be in a position to oast their votes at any time , in the day and they would not need to have the polls kept open any later than five o'clock. My hon. friend says there are two hours which the men could utilize to cast their votes. I know by experience that many employers will say to their employees!: You may go and vote if you like, but we are very busy to-day. They allow them to go and vote between twelve and two o'clock, which does not really give them two 'hours, but one hour. It is impossible to provide for the case of every person, but there are the stationary and electrical engineers, who would find it impossible to cast their votes unless the polls were opened early in the morning. They could not take two hours because they are running the machinery that keeps all industry in motion. The labour men have time and again asked that election day be made a legal holiday. I am sure the country would not suffer if it were declared in the Bill that the day on which a general election-not a bye-election-is held shall be a legal holiday.
Even the business men would find it an advantage to- have a legal holiday, and they would be free to look after the election. My hon. friend may say that we are going to compel the labour men to lose a day. I believe the^ labour men are willing to lose a day provided we have a legal holiday on election day. We may find some employers generous enough to pay the men for th.fr day. I should like to see those employers after the election ; and if we find any we will erect a statue to them.. I believe this will be the best system for everybody.
Mr/ EDWARDS: I cannot e-ee the necessity for the change advocated, 10 p.m. nor do I see the wisdom of it.
Railway men and commercial travellers arei provided for by opening the poll earlier in certain places. The labouring men are provided for because, instead of the poll opening as formerly at nine o'clock and closing at five, it now opens at six o'clock. There is three straight hours. Then they have another hour given them by statute in, addition to their lunch hour at noon. From 200 to 300 men vote at each polling subdivision in cities, and with the poll opening three hours earlier and with 
the hour given by statute in addition to the lunch hour, there should be no congestion in the polling places at any time. It will be found in practice that a considerable portion of the labouring men will vote between six and seven in the morning. We have had no such extension of time as my hon. friend now wants, at previous elections, and the necessity for it has not been shown by any demand from, members on either s-ide of this House.

LAPOINTE: The hon. member points out that we have not had these extensions of time in the past. But to-day we have an opportunity of amending the statute. Ten years' experience has shown that it is necessary to extend the hours of polling during the day. Quebec as a province has done that, and the cities of Qubee have amended their charters extending the hours of polling until eight o'clock, and in some places nine o'clock.
It is not every day that the Dominion Government has ian opportunity of amending the Elections Act. I think that the time for the closing of the poll should be extended to 8 o'clock.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
It would not be in the general interest to extend past 5 o'clock the time during which the poll should remain open. The hours fixed in the Election Act are not of our fixing; they have hitherto been from 9 to 5, a period, of only eight hours. We add three hours in those places where there is need of the additional time; that is a very substantial extension indeed. If the .additional time is added at the end of the day, it does not meet the case of any who are not accommodated by adding the time at the beginning of the day, because the labourer can vote at the beginning just as well as at the end. Moreover, it does away entirely with the opportunity of the traveller and of various classes of railroad labourers to vote. The additional time at the beginning of the day makes more valuable to the labourer the hour that be is entitled to receive from his employer under section 136A, because the poll will not he so crowded during that hour. In the first place, a number of labourers will (have voted between six o'clock and seven or between six o'clock and nine, and, in the next place, a large number of those who would otherwise crowd the poll with him at the noon hour will also have voted. The great rush to get the vote out is immediately upon the opening of the poll. Each party struggles with the other to get the bulk of the vote to the poll early so that as much time

as possible may be allowed for the straggling vote. #

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: What about those who commence work at seven o'clock in the morning?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
Of such persons, those who are able to do so will vote between 6 o'clock and 7. It is true that some may live a long distance away and may not bs able to do that. But they have an extra hour at noon, and that hour will not be so crowded as it was on previous occasions, because large numbers of those who formerly came at that hour will have voted early in the morning. This election will be held, perhaps not in the dead of winter, but at all events when the days are short; and if the time for the closing of the poll is extended from 5 o'clock to 8 there will be a good deal of polling after dark. I do not think that hon. gentlemen on either side of the House want the polls to be open between 6 o'clock and 8 in the winter or in any month that is not near the middle of summer.
As to the suggestion of the member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Verville); I remember its being discussed in the House at length some years ago. There is a good deal to-be said in favour of it. In fact, there is more to be said in favour of a holiday on election day than on some other days when holidays are now given. It would seem to me, however, that there are objections to that course. The excitement that prevails on election day would be intensified a good deal if the whole day were made a holiday. At any rate, the subject is one that is worthy of consideration; so is the suggestion of the member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham). I do not think, however, that either suggestion can be adopted in a Bill that we are going to get though this session. As to the proposal of the member for South Renfrew, the Saskatchewan enactments were sent to me and I have gone thoroughly into them. He is quite right in saying that it has heretofore been impossible for a large number of
travellers and railway men to vote and that hardship has resulted. It is true that the difficulty has been met in Saskatchewan, but in that province there are only two divisional points, whereas in the whole of the Dominion there are 45. To deal with the question in respect of the whole Dominion would necessitate the opening of booths in these 45 divisional points, at which this class oE the population could vote for some five hundred candidates, in 234 Dominion constituencies. The hon. gentlemen will see that tremendous complications would creep in; no matter how perfectly the plan might be worked out, tremendous difficulties in its execution would be involved and great expense incurred. Perhaps the day will come when the difficulty will be met. I think that in the meantime we have met the greater difficulties-iand they will be still more substantially met if the election is held on Monday. I am not in a position to say definitely that it will be held on Monday, but if the election is held in the middle of the week we lose a good deal of the advantage of this new section. So far as I can see now, there is no insuperable objection to holding the election on Monday, and that will be done if possible.

Would it be possible to arrange that a portion of the day be set apart as a holiday for that purpose? I have observed cases where the authority of employers has been exercised viciously - and m a partisan spirit as against their employees who dared to vote. In large cities a man has to vote where he lives, and sometimes his place of occupation is several miles from the place where he must go to vote. Two hours does not give him enough time to get his dinner and go to the place of polling to register his vote.

As to the suggestion that election day be a whole day's holiday, I do not think that ' is desirable because we have found, in certain cities of Ontario in which New Year's day has been .set aside for a municipal election, it has been to tne disadvantage of getting out the vote. The shrinkage has been all the way from twenty-.five to forty per cent of the total vote polled. Might it not be arranged to give the last quarter of the day in addition to the hours which the voter might be allowed to avail himself of at the opening of the polls? If it is a ten-hour day, we might give him the last two and a half hours, and make the last quarter of polling day a legal holiday and let every man off for that time.

daughter of a deserter be not entitled to vote?

Not honourably discharged. Let us read the section:
Every female person shall be capable of voting and qualified to vote at a Dominion election in any province or in the Yukon Territory, who, being a British subject and qualified as to age, race and residence as required in the case of a male person in such province or in the Yukon Territory, as the case may be, is' the wife, widow, mother, sister or daughter of any person,
* but excluding the
wife, widow, mother, sister or daughter of any persons who have deserted from or have been otherwise than honourably discharged from any of such forces.
That can only refer to a member of the forces because the wife, mother, sister, or daughter cannot be discharged from the forces. The only person that can be discharged is a member of the forces, and therefore the reference excluding the relatives of a person means relatives of a soldier who has not been honourably discharged from the forces. I do not see any other meaning that can be taken out of the amendment.

speechtext:
It may be that my
knowledge of the English language is defective, but when I translated this provision into French I found that it led to ambiguity. subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: A woman might have one relative who bad deserted and another who had not. That would he a hard case, but you cannot make a law that would meet every case.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: You can meet that case.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: My hon. friend wants to exclude a deserter and in that I am with him, but I say that the place to exclude .a deserter is in the Military Voters' Act.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: We are not on that Act.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: You are giving the franchise to women in a clause that relates to women only. Under that clause the widow, wife, sister, or mother of the Canadian who has gone overseas to fight will have the right to vote. I am not opposed to disfranchising the deserter, but let that stand aside for the time being, because you will have to amend the rest of the law if you are going to do that. This particular suggestion I made came to my mind because the case of this man Monette. rl happen to know something about the relatives of this man, and I asked myself: Why should these women, who, I am sorry to say, are not deserving of having the vote, even if Monette did go to the front, be given the right of the ballot while the wife of my neighbour, who has been working night and day knitting socks and collecting subscriptions for the Red Cross and the Patriotic Fund should be denied that right? If the theory of the Solicitor General is right, that we should emphasize the right of the .man who has gone to the front to express himself at the polls, and I think it is, it must be remembered that this Bill does not deal with the right of any soldier to vote. It says that the female relatives of any person who has gone to- the front shall have the right to vote. My hon. -friend says that a deserter, or an officer who had not been properly discharged, would be excluded. But they should be dealt with in the Military Voters' Act. Let us put- another section into this Act so that there will be absolutely no ambiguity as to the right of women who are the relatives of soldiers to vote.

But excluding persons Who have deserted from or have been otherwise than honourably discharged from such forces.

Why not put in the

speechtext:
Subsection 2 of
section 1 of the first Bill begins with the following wdrds:
Subject to the provisions of section 5A of this Act, in the compilation of such lists,-
And so on. This Act will be in the hands of many men not accustomed to reading or construing statutes and this section may be confusing. I find that many of my friends on this side have understood this to apply to all the provinces, whereas it is intended to apply only to British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Prince Edward Island. Enumerators reading this may take it as applying to all the provinces.
I would suggest the insertion of the words "in the provinces of British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Prince Edward Island." This would remove any chance of confusion.'	-

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
It applies all over with respect to women. While an enumerator ot deputy returning officer getting only this Act or the old Act might have great diffi-
culty in understanding all of it, as it applies to different provinces in
11 p.m. various ways, the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery is compelled by the law to issue definite and clear instructions to enumerators and returning officers in every province telling them just what does apply to his province. This will all be made clear by instructions from the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
I do not quite agree, and I see no objection to my suggestion by reason of the fact that women must be placed on the list. The same words are used in several sections, section 48 and section 62. The marginal reference to section 62 is "application for certificate as a qualified voter by person whose name is not on list." The sense of that section is that outside of the provinces of Quebec, Ontario, Nova Scotia or New Brunswick, a person claiming the right to vote and not finding his name on the list may apply to the enumerator to have his name entered.
Clearly that could not be done so far as Quebec, Ontario, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia are concerned. It would be made quite clear, I think, by striking out the first and second lines and inserting the words "in the province of British Columbia"-then mentioning all The other provinces.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: It would be clearer if it would be right. In my opinion it would not be right, because the section operates not merely in those provinces, but all over the Dominion; in certain provinces it operates subject to certain limitations. The briefest way of putting it, therefore, is as it is here. I am sure that it will be clearly explained in the instructions issued by the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery.

speechtext: Do you intend to apply the rule at two o'clock in the morning5 Shall all these important amendments be adopted without further discussion?

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: The minister comes here to-night with amendment after amendment which he recognizes as being absolutely necessary to perfect the Bill. It is utterly impossible to discuss this Bill under closure. Amendments have been submitted which alter the Bill, in some cases materially, in other cases not so materially. I understand that at 2 o'clock in the morning closure will be applied, Surely the Bill should not be reported from the committee with these important amendments before it is reprinted for the information of hon. gentlemen. I call the attention of the Secretary of State to the unfairness of dealing with the matter in this way. Does he think that this is an occasion upon which closure should be enforced? Every disposition ihas been shown to facilitate the passage of the Bill; there has not been the slightest attempt to delay it.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: It is quite true that we have been getting on excellently; I hope that we shall so continue. The amendments that have been made, while necessary, do not, in the main, involve discussion. One or two-we have discussed them -simply make the Bill comply with the fundamental principles of the proposed legislation. There is no reason why they should not come in on the last day of the discussion; I have never heard that no amendments should be offered on the last day in committee. There is no question about discussing them. We can discuss them, I freely admit, much better under the ordinary rule in committee, and we have unanimously agreed to do that. But we cannot do it except by unanimous agreement, and I am willing that we should apply the rule rigidly if the Committee so desires.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: Does the minister intend that the closure shall apply at two o'clock in the morning without the Bill being reprinted with the amendments?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
Hon. gentlemen who
have been here know that the amendments are all right. They will be reprinted as soon .as they are decided upon by the committee.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
Before the Bill leaves
the committee stage?

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
