subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
A great many of these
amendments have been made upon the suggestion of the minister himself, and it is grossly unfair to ask the committee to consider tlhem with the closure resolution passed this afternoon staring us in the face. The minister says we cannot consider these amendments after two o'clock. But the minister himself since I came in has occupied three-quarters of the time of the committee in making the necessary explanations-explanations which fie has made with great clearness and with much satisfaction to the committee. What I protest against is that this important Bill should be considered and amended in many different respects under closure procedure.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: Are you going to apply the closure rules, Mr. Chairman?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: No.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: Let us go on as we are.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
I asked the Solicitor
General before six o'clock if it would be possible to provide in the law that-the enumerator should have a residence qualification. Of course, I would prefer that the qualification in Quebec should remain as it is. Every time the lists are made up names can be added by either candidate. The secretary-treasurer does this in our provincial elections. But the Solicitor General does not want to amend the law along that line; it is not such an amendment as he would desire to insert at this time. As I remember the wording of the Bill it says "the Governor in Council may appoint.'' That means that he will appoint.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: This has always been the form. But the Governor in Council has never appointed them.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
That may be, but, as I said this afternoon, this is a thing that is absolutely new to us. We have never had enumerators, and we have never dealt with

them. I would suggest that the enumerators should live in the municipality and, if it were possible, that 'the secretary-treasurer of the municipality should be the enumerator. I think that would be the fairer way because the secretary-treasurer is a man that has some responsibility. He holds his position through the good-will of every inhabitant of the municipality. Perhaps the word "municipality" may seem strange to or scare some of my hon. friends opposite. I understand that in some provinces municipality means the whole county. .

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: That is the case in New Brunswick.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
In Quebec a municipality that has three polling divisions is a very large one. By the word "parish" we mean all the worshippers that belong to a church, and, for administrative purposes, the municipal boundaries are all the same, so that there is in our, province a closer kind of affinity between the people in a municipality on account of our institutions than there is in the other provinces, out West, for instance. The secretary-treasurer, as I said this afternoon,' is thoroughly acquainted with, not only every man and woman in his municipality, but every child. He is at the same time the secretary-treasurer of the school board for the district. I would ask the Solicitor General-this would not take much of an amendment-to insert in the Bill that in Quebec the secretary-treasurer of the municipality shall be the enumerator. The absolute and complete knowledge that he has of his muicipality will make it easier for him to take care of three polls than if you take a man who is not accustomed to going through the assessment rolls and the rolls of the children at school. With men who are accustomed to the work, you would need three men, if each one has to attend to only one poll. The secretary-treasurer is usually ia man of education. He is generally a notary. Sometimes, of course, his duties do not involve much work, because the valuation is only revised. As has been stated 'by some hon. gentleman opposite, the changes in a municipality, especially in an old one, are just the deaths and births, land when the electoral list is revised those who have gone are stricken out and the young men who have reached the age of twenty-one years are added. I make a last appeal to the Solicitor General, not in the way of embarrassing him, nor of delaying the Bill, but in the way of help-

ing along the execution of this law, and of helping along the enfranchisement of the people whom the Bill de-sires to reach and the disfranchisement of those whom the Bill wishes to disfranchise. The secretary-treasurer knows better than any one else when a man of .alien enemy nationality came to the municipality and whether he is naturalized or not. The municipalities are so small, the people are -so close together, .and their relations, I might say, -so intimate, that the secretary-treasurers know the family history of iany one perfectly well. Should the Solicitor General decide that he cannot grant that, I would ask him to add after the words "the Governor in Council" the words "may, in the province of Quebec, appoint an assessor residing within the municipality for which he has to act, or in the neighbouring municipality." We do not want to impose upon other provinces what- we think fight in Quebec.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
That is just the difficulty that has -arisen several times. You cannot make any rule on that point that would be applicable everywhere, and still every .province is just in the .same position, so far as the real substance of the case is concerned, as Quebec. I do not see any formidable objection really to appointing an enumerator from the municipality, nor even -fro-m -the neighbouring municipality, and I venture to -predict that every one will be appointed out from municipality and not even the neighbouring one. One might get a case in- which the right man was just across the road, in which the man everybody would want was the town clerk, perhaps, and could not reside in the municipality. He might reside outside. There would be no gain by my hon. friend's amendment. The great chance is that every one who will be selected wall reside in the municipality because he must reside in the polling division to know his work, to be qualified to do it. I do not like the idea of selecting an individual man and! saying to him: You must d*' this work. That is not the spirit of this Bill. The man, as soon as he is sworn to act, is then bound to act, but it would hardly be right to put the hand of the law on every secretary-treasurer in Quebec, who may, in some oases, be engaged preitty steadily in his own work and may (have other engagements and occupations besides, and say to -him: No matter how busy you are; no matter whether your present time is occupied from morning until night, no matter what sacrifice it may be for you, -for the sake of $30

or (f40 you have to travel through your municipality and enumerate the women in it.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: The secretary treasurers under the provincial law do the work that would correspond to your enumeration. They are making up the lists now. On the 15th those lists have to be posted. I am not afraid of the enumerators, but the people in the municipality are not accustomed to that line of conduct to be followed in order to be registered as electors, and they would be at a loss to know where to' go. They would not understand this new method of procedure, and I am satisfied' that it would not work so easily for the women you want to reach, or the men you want to exclude, as the system I suggest. As far as the work is concerned, I can assure the Solicitor General that none of the secretary-treasurers in any of the rural municipalities will refuse on account of being overworked. I am satisfied they will accept the position.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
The Solicitor General
could comply with my hon. friend's request so far as having the enumerators appointed in the polling division is concerned, because it is a custom in Ontario to appoint the deputy returning officer out of the division, and it would be a matter of common practice to appoint enumerators from the division because there would be no difficulty about getting them. I have no doubt that practice would be followed, and there would be in the division plenty of people perfectly willing to act. If in compiling these lists, say in Ontario, we have to add only certain names and strike off certain names, would the enumerators be likely to go around from house to house to get those names, or would he be subject to the candidates supplying him with names that ought to be added on or taken off?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: It would be his duty to employ both methods, namely, to go from house to house and to accept names from the candidate after investigating each one.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: Or from others?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
Yes. While I am on my feet, I will move the amendment which meets the former request from the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt). I move to amend paragraph (r) of section 1 by striking out from the eighth line of sub-section 3 of section 65 A, provided by said paragraph, the words, "and the," and inserting instead the word "(a)," and by further amending said sub-section by adding after the word "town" in the twelfth
line thereof, the words "and he shall deliver or mail by registered letter a copy of such list to each of the candidates."
While I am on my feet permit me to correct a slight error that I think I made yesterday in referring to the province of Ontario. It is not all the cities and towns over nine thousand that are in the special list of those for whom made-up lists are not now being used, but only county or district towns over nine thousand.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: Is the amendment my hon. friend has just read confined to Ontario?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: That one is, but a previous one did the very same thing for the lest of Canada.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
The greatest objection I have in connection with these enumerators is the great uncertainty as to when and where they shall meet. Section 45 of the old law says:
In the Yukon Territory each enumerator forthwith after taking the said oath, shall post up in six of the most public places within each polling division for which he has been appointed enumerator, a notice that he has been appointed enumerator for the polling division, and that he will proceed forthwith to compile, and within thirty days will complete the voters' list for the polling division, and designating the office or place within one of such polling divisions where he may in the meantime be found, and the hours during which he will attend at suoh office or place for the purpose of compiling such list on each lawful day, which shall begin not later than ten o'clock in the forenoon and end not earlier than four o'clock in the afternoon each day.
2. In such notice the time and place during and at which the final revision of the lists for which provision is hereinafter made will take place, shall be designated.
That is the law for the Yukon. If something along this line were done for the province of Nova Scotia, so that we would know when and where these men were to begin work, I should be satisfied.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: There has always been a corresponding section to this for Alberta and Saskatchewan, and that section is now applicable to all the provinces of Canada.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: Which section is it?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: I cannot give it just now, but it is further amended by providing for the posting up of the lists for a longer period during which the enumerator sits to revise the lists, and for a longer period between the time of revision and election day.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: The posting is required to be done in only two places. That is a very limited notice.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: That is the way the posting is always done in those provinces. In addition to that we are compelling the ennmerator to send a separate list by registered mail to each candidate in each constituency on the very day he posts up the lists. The candidates get a list, and they can make copies if they want to.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: I think two is a very small number.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: It must be remembered that in the rural parts they have no way of typewriting the list, but there is nothing to hinder the candidates from making a copy.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: A copy will be sent to the candidates fifteen days before polling?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
Yes. I wish to move in amendment to section 2:
That section 136 of the present Bill, subsection (b) of section 2, be amended by adding the names of the following cities:	Stratford,
St. Thomas, Saskatoon, Moosejaw, Kingston, Brockville and Hull.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: Would my hon. friend object to adding Woodstock also?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: I do not think there is any objection to adding any place so long as the member for the constituency is sure that the convenience is going to be greater than the inconvenience.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: It does not make a great deal of difference.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
My hon. friend from
Westmorland (Mr. Copp) is not in his seat at the moment, but I imagine he would like to have Moncton added to the list. It is a great railway centre and, I think it would be desirable to have the polls open an hour earlier there.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: We will add Moncton.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: I think Brockville is a city for the purposes of the provincial Act.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: Naming it as a city makes it a city for the purposes of this Act.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
In the case of a tied ballot, on a recount the judge decides whether the voter who has been refused a certificate by the enumerator had the right to vote in a certain polling division. It might happen that the tied voter might'not have the right to vote in a certain polling division on ao count of not being a resident there, hut he might have the right to vote in the electoral district.
[Mr. Pugsleyl

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: If that were permitted and if a man wanted to vote in some more convenient place than where he had the right to vote, all he would have to do would be to force his vote through and the judge would have to count it. We do not want to enable a man to vote out of his division.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: I want to ask one or two questions which are not actually iq line with the subjects which have been under discussion this evening, but perhaps I might get attention. What is the position of Douk-hobors who have left the community and have taken up residence as ordinary citizens? Are they free from the prohibition of the Act, or are they still under the terms of the Act?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: In my opinion, they are free from the prohibition of the Act.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: Could that ruling or that view be expressed in any way for the information and guidance of the enumerators?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: Yes, it could be, by the instructions which, the Act provides, shall be sent out by the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery. The disfranchisement provisions of this Act are intended to cover only Douk-hobors and Mennonitee who are included in the exemptions under the Military Service Act, and not other Doukhobors and Mennonites or other classes who* are not conscientious objectors, so that the Doukhobors and Mennonites who are not members of the community, if they do not come in as conscientious objectors, would not be subject to this Act. There is no difllculty in making that clear by instructions issued by the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery. Of course, I realize I should be very careful about giving my opinion to . the House on matters of law. I simply give this as my opinion as a lawyer. Personally, I have not the least doubt about it.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: I am not as familiar with the situation in regard to the Mennonites, but I rather fancy it is somewhat similar. There are Mennonites who, although they call themselves Mennonites, do not hold to the original non-combatant principles of "Cue sect. I should think similar action would be desirable in their case.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: I think so, too.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: I understand that ia man of alien enemy descent is debarred from voting, no matter in what country he was born.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: Not unless his natural language is an alien enemy language.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: My hon. friend is aware that there are large numbers of people of German descent, born in the United States, who are now residents of Canada.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: They are not affected by this Act at all. Any born in the United States, no matter what language they speak, are not affected by the Act.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: The word "European" is used?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: Yes. I wish to move that the cities of Charlottetown and Belleville be added to- the list I moved in my last amendment.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
Has the question of the secrecy of the vote been very carefully considered, according to article 62?
Mr, MEIGHEN: Yes.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: Suppose the enumerator gave a certifidate to a woman, entitling her to vote at a certain polling station. The deputy returning officer takes the vote, and he is obliged, according to the law, to record the name of that woman in a book. Now, suppose only one woman votes and that vote has to be put in an envelope, where is the secrecy?

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: She will tell anyway.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: I am afraid in that case my hon. friend is right. If there was only one woman in the poll, and her vote had to be enveloped, and it came before a recount judge, I am afraid the public would know for whom she voted, if the judge decided she had the right to vote. If he did not so decide, the public would not know.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
If the committee will turn to section 32 of the Bill distributed to-day, they will see it reads as follows:
32. The qualifications necessary to enable any male person to vote at a Dominion election in any province shall, except as by this Act otherwise provided, be those established by the laws of that province as necessary to entitle such male person to vote in the same part of the province at a provincial election.
Section 33A says that the qualification of a woman shall be the same as to age, race, and residence as that of a man. In the ordinary lists prepared in past elections, the provincial qualification and the provincial machinery were available, and the lists were prepared pursuant to provincial legislation. In all the provinces, I think, to be
364J
a voter a person must be a British subject and twenty-one years of age. As this Act is altogether independent of the electoral' machinery of the provinces, the electoral, machinery of the provinces will never begin to work, therefore there is no data oh wlfich one can determine how long* a person must have residence in the province or in the municipality to be entitled to vote. For the sake of illustration, take the province of Ontario.
At the last session of the Ontario legislature a change -was made in the conditions under which a man might ,be placed upon [DOT] the voters' lists. Prior to that if he was-entitled to vote at a 'municipal, and not at a legislative election, he would be put on the list provided that he had been in the province for nine months prior to the assessor beginning his duties or twelve months prior to the revision of the list by the jndge. If, on the other hand, he was a manhood suffrage voter, he would be put on the legis

Lative list if he had been one year in Canada and three months in the municipality. These provisions will, however, under this Act, never come into effect as the provincial' legislative machinery in Ontario intended to apply' to the province will not be effective, and therefore in order to make provision for residence and domicile qualfi- ' cation it is necessary that there should be an amendment to, this Act. I, therefore, beg to move:
That section 1, paragraph (c), be amended by adding as subsection 2 and 3 of section 32 the following:
"2. Except in the province of Quebec and notwithstanding anything in this Act contained, in preparing or adding to the voters' lists pro-' vided for by this Act, the qualifications as to residence, and domicile of electors shall In any [DOT] province where there is no relevant or applicable provision to the contrary be residence for one year in Canada and residence and domi- ' cile in the electoral district for thirty days, both of said periods to be fixed by reference to the date of the writ of eleotion. '
The purpose of the amendment is that in any province outside of Quebec the elector must have resided, in Canada for one year and in the electoral district for thirty-days prior to the date of the writ of election being issued.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: That would be applicable: to women voting in Ontario?

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
To a very great extent.'
It would apply also to cities and county towns where the population is over 9,000.' In Quebec there has to be a variation for the reason that their law has no qualifi

cation as to residence in Canada or residence-within the electoral district. All that is'

[DOT]necessary is that the elector shall at the time of the preparation of the -lists be domiciled in the electoral district. Therefore the second amendment reads as follows:
3. In the province of Quebec notwithstanding anything in this Act contained the qualification as to domicile shall be domicile at the date of the saift writ of election.
A person must be domiciled in Quebec [DOT]at the time the enumerator makes his rounds.
Mr. MeCREA:	I notice that there are
certain towns and cities to be put on the list where the voting will commence at six o'clock in the morning. These are manufacturing and railway points. Sherbrooke is a manufacturing and railroad centre, and I think it would be well to put it on the list of places where the poll will be open at six o'clock.	[DOT]

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: I will have it added to the clause.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
Is it
the pleasure of the committee that Sherbrooke shall be added?

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: Carried.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
It strikes me that the
*amendments proposed by the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. NiCkle) are so very important in their character that they should not be pressed to-night. Take that affecting the province of Quebec for instance; there are very few members from Quebec here to-night. The leader of the Opposition is absent. It is intended to depart in some way from the provincial lists. If it is not intended this amendment Would not be *moved by my hon. friend. He >is moving it because he is taking some position different from that which is in the Quebec law. Section 32 provides that:
32. The qualifications necessary to enable any male person to vote at a Dominion election in any province shall, except* as by this Act otherwise provided, be those established by the laws of that province as necessary to entitle such male person to vote in the same part of the province at a provincial election.
Why is it necessary , at this late hour for the hon. member to propose an amendment to alter the principle laid down by the Solicitor General that the provincial law as to the voters' lists should apply? If this makes any change it is of a most important character. If it does not make a change, if it simply carries out the provincial law, there is no necessity for it. I would ask my hon. friend whether he thinks an amendment of that character should be pressed without giving an opportunity to members from the

province of Quebec to discuss it. ' I do not quite understand what the other amendment with reference to the rest of the Dominion means.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: The object of these provisions is merely to cover possible cases of omission. As has been explained by my hon. friend from Kingston (Mr. Nickle), on account of certain legislation passed by the legislature of Ontario at the last session, the provisions fixing the period of residence would not be applicable in the case of lists which are to be made up in cities and towns. Therefore, this provision seems necessary. As far as Quebec is concerned, it is not intended to affect the provincial law but is simply to carry it out. In Quebec, the qualification is domicile at the time the list is being made, but as the provincial law may not apply to the lists made under this Act the same principle is established here; that is domicile at the time the list is made up.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: No, this is changed apparently. The domicile in Quebec is of the date of the writ of the election.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: That is when the list is made up.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
As I understand the
amendment, this would apply to women who are to be added in the townships and towns in Ontario, and also in the towns of over 9,000 where registration takes place.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: So far as Ontario is cor cerned, I agree that it is a necessary amendment.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: Why not limit it to Ontario? There is no difficulty in the other provinces because there is the qualification. In New Brunswick one qualification is as to residence or ownership of property. If the provincial lists are to be followed, there is no necessity to make any change. Why not make the amendment apply simply to the province of Ontario?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
I do not think that would be wise. The necessity of the amendment arose by reason of attention being called to the peculiar condition of the legislation of Ontario. Argument might be made that there was no relevant provision in Ontario. We cannot be sure that some similar condition does not prevail in other provinces. This section has no application except in the case where there is im relative and applic-

able legislation in the province. If there is relevant legislation, in any province, that prevails. If for any reason it appears that legislation in the province is not in force for this particular purpose, then this Act has application, but not otherwise.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: I do not think there is necessity for this amendment in our province, as a man has no right to be put on the list unless he is domiciled in the district.	[DOT]

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: This amendment has been prepared by the Minister of Justice, whom we consulted, and who said, as my hon. friend has said, that the legislation of Quebec requires that there shall be domicile at the time when the list is in preparation; but that provision of the provincial law may not have application to a list which would be made up under this Act, and therefore, in order to carry out the absolute and necessary intent of the provincial law, this amendment is proposed which declares that, domicile at the time the list is made up, that is at the date of the writ of election, shall be the controlling qualification.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: But if a man from the province of Quebec leaves the province and is away for a year he has no more right to vote, by the law.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
This does not
change that.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: We are at present making our lists in Quebec. They will be deposited by the 15th. Complaints may then be made until the 30th of September, after which time the council of every municipality has fifteen days to re-12 m. vise the list. A man to be on our list must be domiciled in a polling district.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: The Act does not touch lists as already established in Quebec except as they are to be changed by the addition of women voters and by the disqualification of voters of enemy nationality. In fixing domicile for the women voters it is necessary to have this provision which is established upon the same basis as that which ordinarily prevails in the province of Quebec in the preparation of the provincial lists.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
Section 48 says that the enumerators shall post up copies. There is no appeal, so far as counties are concerned, from the enumerators. There is an appeal in cities an towns of 9,000 or over.
These appeals must be in within three days, which is too short a period.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: That has been changed to four days.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
And the ten days has
been changed to fifteen days. The times are all too short. When there are enumerators appointed absolutely of one political opinion, who can make up a list just to suit themselves, it is an absolutely wrong thing to tie any party down to the decision of enumerators. I should like those in charge of this measure to look at section 48. Where is the appeal? There is none, excepting to the enumerator [DOT]on election day.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: The enumerator's work is revised in every respect judicially. Everything he does in any province, if it is wrong, can be corrected by the opposing party before a judge.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: After the election.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: Before the election is decided. I will be quite happy in my constituency if I can be declared-

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: Yes, because the enumerator will he of your political faith and will fix the lists to suit you. That is the object of the Bill.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman believes what he says-

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: I believe absolutely what I say; and that is why the Bill is being passed.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: You should have sympathy with us during all these twelve years in the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan. It is strange the hon. member did not look so fierce and talk so wildly in those days.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: Because the Act was being administered honestly.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: Oh, I see.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: I would like an answer showing what provision there is for an appeal from the enumerator in counties.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
First of all, the Act will be administered honestly. Next, if any enumerator makes an error intentionally or otherwise, if he puts a man off who should not be off, the other side can challenge that vote and demand that, before it be counted, a judge shall say it is right. If he refuses to put a man on who should be on, that man can defy him, demand a certificate, go to the

poll, take the oath and vote, and his vote is counted unless the judge decides it is not a proper vote. The residue that will come before the judge, it is believed, will be the smallest residue that could in justice go.
It is the only way you can get review; it is the only way you can get your lists in country districts ready in time for an election. If you have judicial review in every country district you cannot have the election within a reasonable time. We provide for having the election within a reasonable time and at the same time provide such Safeguards that no enumerator can make an error without the other side having 'ample opportunity to correct it. I do not think it makes any difference whether the judge gives his decision before or after the election, so long as his decision is a proper one. It has the same result so far as the contest is concerned.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
Why should you not
have appeals in rural districts as well as in cities and towns?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: There are not judges enough; you could, not get the work done. Does the hon. gentleman, know how long ' the work takes now in rural districts?

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: I do know very well.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: In the northern parts of Ontario, for example, it takes three months.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: You propose to leave all these questions to a recount after the election, is held. It seems to me that is an absurd proposal. Why should there not be an appeal before the election. You have thirty days between nomination day and polling day. Why should not the lists be made up at least by nomination day? Surely the judge in any constituency can decide in twenty days whether or not the lists are properly made up.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: In many instances he could not get around.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: Well, give him an opportunity to get around.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman know that in some constituencies-

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: I know as much about the constituencies as the hon. gentleman does; perhaps I know more. The proposal with regard to appeal is absurd and absolutely wrong.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
Section 33A, page 1, provides that a woman who is the wife, widow,

mother, sister or daughter of any person, male or female, living or dead, who is serving or has served without Canada in any of the military forces, shall be entitled to vote. Is it not desirable that there should be a direction to the enumerator that he should take knowledge of the name and identity of the soldier in regard to whom a woman claims the right to vote? If the name of the soldier in whose name a woman claims the right to vote is placed on the enumeration list along with her name, there would be no question, in case of challenge, about her right to vote.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: That would encumber the list quite a little, but if it produced any substantial results, there would be a compensation. I do not think, however, that it would produce any substantial results. If the vote is challenged, all these details must come before the judge in any case. It is a question whether the judge's duty would be in any way lightened or anything would be made any more definite before the judge by the presence of the name of the soldier after her name on the list.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: If there is no direction to the enumerator all he is required to do is to ask the women: Are you entitled to vote? Have you a brother, son or other relative at the front? She says: yes, and he puts her name down, he is not required to pursue the question of identity. If there was a direction that he must pursue the question of identity, it might save troublesome proceedings later on and tend to the securing of a better and more definite list.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: I am inclined to think that the hon. member is right. It would be better to have the instructions to the enumerator include the duty on his part of keeping a record of the name of the soldier.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: Could not my hon. friend go further than that and devise some method of establishing the identity of the person claiming relationship?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: Every person's identity is put beyond doubt on the list, The directions would be to get the name of the soldier.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: As this discussion goes on I recall from time to time the evidence given before the Returned Soldiers Committee. I have in mind a statement made by the Chairman, who was also Chairman of the Patriotic Fund, that in any number of cases two or three women claimed to be the wife of one man.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: The identity of the women is to be established by every possible means. Her name goes on the list; she has a number; her occupation and address are given. I do not think there is any way of more clearly fixing her identity.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: Surely some proof ought to be required.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
The Prime Minister
says that the amendment which has been moved by the member for Kingston (Mr. Rickie) was prepared by the Minister of Justice. To whom should its authorship be attributed? /

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
This amendment arose
merely out of my .desire to do a kindly thing to the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Car-veil), who was intensely bitter before recess because there was no provision preventing men who had been out of New Brunswick for nine years, and1 who had gone to the United States, from voting. This was done in order to try to prevent the evil of which he complained.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
That may be correct as to other provinces, but I am speaking now of Quebec. I cannot understand this provision ;
In the province of Quebec, notwithstanding anything in this Act contained, the qualification as to domicile shall he domicile on the date of the said writ of election.
The Prime Minister, in answer to the hon. member for Bagot (Mr. Marcile), said that this would apply only to the new voters, but it does not only apply to them; it is general; it would apply to all. The result of this would be, it seems to me, that a voter whose name was on the list and who changed his domicile, perhaps a month before the date of the said writ of election, would be disqualified, and as he would not be on any other list, he would lose his vote altogether. I dislike intruding myself in any matter relating to another province, but the matter has to be dealt with as this is an important amendment and it is so late in the discussion. If the minister would change this to read-	*
In the province of Quebec, notwithstanding anything in this Act contained, the qualification of the female voters to be added under this Act as to domicile shall be domicile on the date of the said writ of election.
I would see no objection, hut in the form proposed by the minister it might disqualify <a large number of people who would find themselves challenged at the polls because they had changed their domicile, and as
they would not be on any other list would thereby lose their vote altogether.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: If I understood the Prime Minister correctly, the proposed form would not be objectionable, but I would like to consult either the Prime Minister or the Minister of Justice before definitely accepting that amendment.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: I was not in the House when the amendment was moved, and I did not hear the explanation of the Prime Minister, but it seems to me that it really applies to all the voters, because section 32 applies to any male person qualified to vote at a Dominion election. This amendment would, therefore, apply to all voters already on the ist of Quebec. There is certainly no reason whatever for this amendment.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: If hon. gentlemen will refer to section 65 A on page 8 of the original Bill, they will see that there is nothing in their contention. The Minister of Justice, who drew this sub-section-of course, I do not understand the law in Quebec- explained it to me. He said that in Quebec, the qualification of the elector is determined by his domicile as of the date on which the lists are deposited with a certain official who has charge of the lists- I do not know just what his title is.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: The clerk of the municipality and the town clerk of the city.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: That applies to the male voters in Quebec, those who are entitled to vote at a parliamentary election. But the lists on which the female voters in Quebec will vote will never be deposited with any official because the provisions of the Quebec law do not make that possible, and therefore, there must be some date determining domicile. As the list in reference to the male voter would be prepared so that the provisions of sub-section of 65 A would not apply, it was not necessary to say anything further on that point of the argument, and this sub-section 3, as I understand it, will apply only to the female voters. Whether or not there is any objection to putting in the word "female," I do not know what the Minister of Justice will say. This subsection 3 was put in with a view to only affecting women voters added under this measure.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: If it applies only to female voters, let us say that, and then there will be no objection. [DOT]

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
This section says that in the preparation of and the adding to the

lists, the qualification shall be domicile on the day of election. I can understand why, in respect to new voters you should make that provision, but the difficulty is in the interpretation of it. A man who had changed his domicile prior to the date of the writ could be challenged and his name would be struck off, and as he would not be on any other list, he would lose his vote. That is what I am afraid would be the result of this amendment.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: Section 65A begins with the words, "Notwithstanding anything in this part of this Act." This amendment says again: "Notwithstanding anything in this Act." That bars section G5A, and the question of domicile will be settled as from the date of the issue of the writ. I did not read the section very closely, but it would be better if you struck out the words, "Notwithstanding anything in this Act contained," and just say, "In the province of Quebec, the qualification as to domicile shall be domicile on the date of the said writ of election." Do the words, "Notwithstanding anything in this Act contained" refer to the whole Act or to subsection 65AP

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
They have
general application. The object of the section prepared by the Minister of Justice is to preserve, in relation to additions which are to be made to this list, the same principle which is enacted by the law of Quebec with regard to the preparation of the ordinary lists of that province. In the ordinary lists, qualification as to residence is settled by the domicile at the time the lists are made up. This amendment is designed to maintain that principle in respect to additions made of women voters to this list. That is the sole purpose of it. It was thought necessary by the Minister of Justice, who can explain it much more fully that I can as he is more familiar with the laws of the province of Quebec than I can claim to be.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
When my right hon.
friend was out I raised this point. The amendment says:

speechtext: This is a section that I thought could be delegated while I was attending to others, and I have not followed it from the beginning. I have listened to the argument pretty carefully, and I hope it will be found that the words can be inserted. My idea is that they can be.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
As to the purpose of the amendment itself, before we discuss where it ought to be put, as the Prime Minister has explained with regard to these female voters to be added to the lists, the date of domicile must correspond with the ordinary law of the province. By section 180 of the Quebec Election Act it is provided that,
The following persons, and no others, being males, and who, at the time of the deposit of the list under articles 196 and 197, or 22-2 and 223-
I may say that this provision is for Montreal and the divisions outside of Montreal.
-as the case may be, are domiciled within the limits of the municipality in the electoral district for which the list is made.
With regard to the ordinary lists there is. no requirement as to period of residence in the constituency. You are entitled to be on the list, so far as domicile is concerned, if you were domiciled in the constituency at the time the list was deposited with the secretary treasurer, or with the City Clerk. With regard to these women who are to be put on the lists, they only get put on the lists when this enumeration takes place, and absolutely the same principle is applied. If you are domiciled in the constituency at the time

the list- is being made, that is the constituency you belong to, and on the list for that constituency you are entitled to be put. We have fixed on the date of the issue of the writ of election, because that is the time when these additions to the original list are taking place.

speechtext: Why not specify "female voters"?	-

I do not see why any difficulty should arise when he -swears he is not disqualified. He is qualified because he is on the list for that electoral constituency, whether he has moved out or not.

We have not changed
that in the slightest. Th-at is the form which has been always there.
Mr. L. A. LAPOINTE. But to-day it is one man one vote, and the elector votes where he resides.

speechtext:
There are certain restrictions suggested by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) and the hon. member for -Carleton (Mr. Carvell).
I think my hon. friend does well to wait until we are pretty weary before asking that thi-s section be adopted, because every man who is at -all awake and alert must see there is the -strongest possible objection to the section in its present form. I find it provides that the relatives of any person who is serving within Canada in- any of the naval forces shall be entitled to vote.

After the Act passes, I suppose there will be four weeks before the election, and of course you can see the absurdity of allowing it to apply to relatives of persons who may join the naval forces after the election.

The hon. member for

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: I am sure the Secretary of State misunderstood the hon. member for Carleton.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: That'is what he said.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
I do not believe anything the minister could do in the way of slight amendments of this character would convince the hon. member for Carleton of the sincerity of this Government in submitting this Bill to Parliament. I would ask my hon. friends on this side of the House if they heard the hon. member for Carleton say he would be satisfied as to the sincerity of the Government. There is no corroboration of that statement. The amendment is a slight concession to the demand for not violating all the rules that ought to govern in connection with the giving of votes to the relatives of the soldiers. The Secretary of State has spoken of the Bill as based upon a principle, which appeals very strongly to every man-that those who have gone to the front occupy a unique position. He says they have either made or are ready, to make the supreme sacrifice for the country; that many have died upon the battlefield; and that it is only right that their relatives might be supposed in a certain measure to be able to speak for them, and it is but proper their relatives should be given the right to vote. He based it upon the grounds of service and of sacrifice.
Yet he allows the relatives of, I presume, hundreds of men who have joined vessels engaged in the fishery service to vote-vessels which now are part of the naval forces of Canada, and also men on cruisers, cooks, engineers, and others who had been employed on these vessels for years before the war broke out, who never thought of going abroad, who are engaged upon vessels that could not sail or steam' across the Atlantic, and who, when they joined, knew that their services would be entirely in Canada. These men are simply doing the work that they were employed to do years ago and their

engagement involves no liability to cross the ocean, to go to the front or to incur the risk or make the sacrifices which men who have gone to the front are called upon to make. The relatives of these officers and men, seamen, midshipmen, cooks, engineers and deck hands, are, by this Act, to have the right to vote. I do not know what argument has been presented in favour of doing this, but it cannot be justified upon any of those grounds which the Secretary of State and the Prime Minister have so eloquently put forward as the reason for giving the votes .to relatives of those who have gone overseas. In the case of the soldier, of the man who enlists, hut who has not left Canada, who has volunteered for the service of his country and is ready to cross the ocean and risk his life on the battlefield, this privilege is not extended to his relatives. It is only when he goes overseas that his relatives shali be entitled to vote. Yet, that principle is departed from in regard to men who are engaged upon these vessels which constitute a part of the Canadian naval service. Why should that be so? Why should the relatives of a man who has enlisted in the expeditionary forces of Canada as an infantryman, an artilleryman, or as the member of a forestry battalion, and who has signified his willingness to go to the front and risk his life, be debarred from the right to vote because he is still in Canada, while you give the right to the relatives of the men who are engaged upon these vessels, who have not gone out of Canada, who never intend to go and who know that they will not have to go?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is quite wrong. A man who joins the naval service has to go wherever he is sent, whether overseas or elsewhere. When the hon. gentleman says that these men never volunteered to go overseas he is wrong.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: They never expect to go.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: The figures given to-day show that some 3,000 have gone. With regard to the rest of the hon. gentleman's address, I have answered it so often that I think he would consider me a bore if 1 answered it again.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
The minister has not
answered. The minister says that they have volunteered to go overseas. So did the infantrymen and the artillerymen volunteer to go overseas.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: That is quite true.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: They have all volunteered to go overseas. But there are a great many small vessels forming the naval forces in Canada-is that not so? Are not the fishery cruisers a paTt of the naval forces of Canada?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: The naval forces were defined clearly this afternoon Dy the Minister of Marine and Fisheries.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
They would include the men I spoke of. It cannot he that because they have volunteered and are liable to be sent overseas the right is given to their relatives and refused to men who have volunteered in the military forces of Canada to go overseas. They are compelled by the oath which they take to go beyond the seas, and they volunteered for that purpose. Why should their relatives be refused the vote while the relatives of the men who are serving on board these vessels, who are still in Canada and many of whom have never been outside of Canada except perhaps for a few miles along the coast, be given the vote?
I am not able to see the reason.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman desires the relatives of the soldiers in Canada to be included it can very easily be done by simply striking out the words "without Canada." If the hon. gentleman cares to move that amendment we will give it immediate consideration.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
That is not what I am at. The Government limit the right of the female relatives of soldiers- to the relatives of those men beyond the seas. That is the principle of the Bill. I take it that, for good and sufficient reasons as they appear to the Government, they do that as a matter of principle because their view is that if men are still in Canada they will be able to vote and there will not be the same diffi

culty about it as there may be in the case of the soldiers at the front. I hope that difficulty will not occur in very many cases.
I trust that all the soldiers will have an opportunity of casting their ballots and determining how the affairs of this country will be administered during the next five years, and whether the mismanagement, corruption, partisanship and waste of public money shall be continued during the next five years or not. Now the Government refuse the privilege to female relatives of the members of the expeditionary forces who have not left Canada.
But with respect to those in the naval forces, the relatives of those who have
served either within or without Canada are given the vote. My hon. friend may have explained the reasons for this distinction very fully and satisfactorily. He certainly did not do so when I had the good fortune to be present; and I should be delighted, and I am sure the country would be, if the minister could give any satisfactory explanation for this distinction. I cannot conceive of any. We have still an hour before the guillotine will fall, and I invite the minister to explain this discrimination. He invites me to suggest amendments. We have been -considering this Bill hour after hour, a Bill which, when it was presented to this committee, gave evidence of as careless drafting-perhaps not careless but of as hasty drafting-as any Bill ever presented to this House. When the Bill was introduced at was incomplete, it was interlined, it was not completely printed, and it was in such form that it could not be printed in French until the very day of the second reading. This Bill, drafted and introduced in imperfect foTm, was not distributed in French and English until after the calling of the second reading, owing to the haste of its preparation. To-day the minister has presented amendment after amendment, a'l under the rules of closure which, if they had been applied, would have absolutely prevented any discussion of these amendments or of the Bill. I would ask the minister during the remaining hour to explain the discrimination in 33 A between the female relatives of those who have joined the expeditionary force and are still in Canada training to go overseas to fight for their country, and the relatives of those who are members of the naval force who are still in Canada and will be at the time of the election.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: It is quite true that there is an hour yet before the closure comes into effect, and I know that the hon. member is troubled as to keeping up the discussion for that time. We are all good-natured on this side, and do not at all mind his occupying-

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: I can assure you that we feel very ill-natured on this side. This is one of the greatest outrages ever perpetrated.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
I would rather the hon. member would not ask me to repeat myself to help him out in occupying this hour. I have explained every point that he has brought up. We have no particular objection to enfranchising the relatives ot soldiers in Canada if hon. gentlemen opposite desire them to have the franchise. Bui

there-is a difference between them and those who are overseas. There would be an opportunity for fraudulent enlistment for male fide or not bona fide enlistment. There has been some of that in Canada, not a great deal.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: That is the way you would get recruits.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
Recruits that are not bona fide are not much good if they afterwards leave. I accepted the suggestion of the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Car-vell) with reference to the patrol service in Canada. Those in Canada as
1 a.m. yet are not subject in any degree to the perils of war. Those enlisted in the naval forces are, although some of them are not in as great danger as others; many of the overseas forces, construction and forestry battalions, are in the same position, although the peril there is very substantial indeed. It is very substantia] in the naval force too.
Mr. A. K- MACLEAN: Are the vessels engaged originally in the fishery service now within the naval service?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: I shall ask the minister.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: What is the sense of asking that? Every man who enlists for service in this war takes the oath for the war and becomes a soldier or sailor for the war.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: What has that to do with it?

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext: Just to create trouble the hon. member desires to send for the minister to give that information.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
My hon. friend does not understand my statement. I want to know if the ships that are actually engaged in the fishery service, by the statute become part of the Canadian navy. There are on the Great Lakes a number of vessels engaged in the fisheries service; does my hon. friend say they are performing war service?
Mr. 'CURRIE:	The man who enlists in
the naval service, is sworn in and put on the regular patrol is performing war service. By no 6tretch of the imagination could the hon. gentleman look upon these men as not belonging to the navy.
Mr. A. K. MA'OLEAN: Suppose they do; is it right that their relatives should have the vote?

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
The question resolves
itself into whether these men will vote for hon. gentlemen oippo-site. If they would

not vote for hon. gentlemen opposite, it would be very wrong to give them the vote; that is what is disturbing the member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean). Many of those men are doing mine-sweeping service on the coast, where submarines have been active. A gentleman whom I met in the hotel last evening told me that the ship upon which he had been bound to Quebec was sent to Halifax when it reached the Banks because of the report that there might be submarines in the mouth of the St. Lawrence. The most dangerous service rendered in connection with the war is mime-sweeping,-looking after mines dropped by submarines. Thousands of young men in 'Scotland and England have been blown up in these trawlers. I received a letter the other day in which it was stated that a young man 22 years of age had been drowned when a trawler that he was on was blown up. Many of these ships go out, strike a mine, and are never seen again. The Germans have submarines in the Atlantic that are capable of coming to this side and of carrying large quantities of mines for distribution around the mouths of harbours. Submarines have attacked vessels off the Atlantic coast of the United States. Men engaged in the very service of which my hon. friend complains have been lost at sea. Why, then, does he desire to discriminate against them? The wives, daughters, sisters amd mothers of those men are as much entitled to the right to vote as to the right to receive separation allowance. The member for 'St. John has talked so much this session; he has asked so many ' questions, that he really exhausts the frontbenchers on this side. I am sure that he must have asked millions of questions since the session commenced. The member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) also has distinguished himself by his attacks on members on this side, particularly by his venomous attacks on the Government. When I see a man in action in this House I always visualize something that he resembles. There is a modern instrument which is employed in the building art and which is operated by means of compressed air and mud-. This instrument is known as a mud-gun, and if there is one thing that the member for North -Cape Breton reminds me of, it is a mud-gun. The trouble is that when he starts in he does not confine himself to operations above the belt. He indulges in all kinds of insults and insinuations, and he gets away with them because we do not want to -waste the time-

of the House in answering 'him. The volumes of Hansard he has filled this session will go down to posterity, but at the conclusion of this session I have no 'doubt that we shall have seen the last of him for ten years.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
If the member for
North iSimcoe (Mt. Currie) thinks that it is a soft snap to put me out of action in my county, I invite him down to North Cape Breton and Victoria. The honourable gentleman is the last man in this country, in view of the record that the ex-Minister of Militia gives him, who should talk about action.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
Now, he is starting the
mud business.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
If my honourable
friend wants to know his record as a man in action, I may tell him that he was found up to his neck in a dugout when he should have been at the front leading his men. When he came to this country looking for promotion the then Minister of Militia refused to give him promotion, because he was not entitled to it. Afterwards the honourable gentleman stood up in this House and complained about it. For a number of months the honourable gentleman was too much ashamed of himself to mention soldiers or soldiering. Now he is getting Dutch courage; he thinks that people are forgetting his record. What right has he to turn on me at this hour of the night? I have been perfectly quiet during the last twenty-four hours. My honourable friend puts himself forward as a man whose intellect towers over that of other honourable gentlemen in this House, but be is the only person who thinks he occupies that position. So far as wasting powder on dead monkeys is concerned, I think I have put in almost enough time on my honourable friend. If he thinks that he can fling mud at me whenever he wants to, he is mistaken; he bad better, take to his dugout. He says that I have insulted the 'Government and the members of the House. I am not aware, Sir, that I have insulted any member of this House since I came into it. I do not take kindly to insults from anybody. I do not expect them; I do not take them, because I am not built along those lines, either mentally or physically. What I do not take from other people, I am not disposed to pass over to them. I am disposed to get along amicably and respec-fully with every member of this House, and
I shall be sorry, indeed, to have it go abroad amongst hon. members that I am insulting the Government or insulting any member of this House. If I believe the Government is wrong, or ifs I have any criticism, I make it in clear cut, bad Anglo-Saxon very often, because I must say to hon. gentlemen that, when I stand up here speaking English, I am not speaking my native tongue. When an hon. member from Quebec addresses the House, if he makes mistakes in his English, it is all excused because English is not his native tongue, but if a man who is a Gaelic man as I am, makes any mistake, it is attributed to stupidity on his part. I am serious when I say that English is not my native tongue. I am not, therefore, as flowery as some hon. gentlemen might be in the use of that language, but I can make myself understood, particularly when I am saying some things about hon. gentlemen who occupy the treasury benches. What I wish to say about the Bill now before the House-

speechtext: Say it in Gaelic.

speechtext:
The hon. member for
Calgary, (Mr. R. B. Bennett), who is not in the House now, broke forth the other night into some of St. Paul's injunctions and directions-

speechtext: Oh, oh.

speechtext: Say it in Gaelic.

spiritual wickedness in high places. I am asked to speak Gaelic. I am also going to follow some of St. Paul's directions, namely, not to cast pearls before swine. To be serious for a moment-
