speechtext:
The hon. member for
North Simcoe, (Mr. Currie) understands me in Gaelic well enough. I have spoken Gaelic to him before, and perhaps he thought that was a weakness in me, and that was why he turned his mud-gun on me, the only gun he can handle.
There is in our constitution a provision which recognizes civil rights as property. The right to vote is, in a sense, property. The minister is giving the enumerators power to strike men off the lists without giving them notice or an opportunity of defence. That is not right. If some day, when the minister is not very busy, he will open the first volume of the reports of the Supreme Court of Canada and read the first case reported there, he will find this doctrine of notice dealt with at length,

and the doctrine laid down that a British subject cannot legally be deprived of anything that is in the nature of property or civil rights without giving him notice that he is to be so deprived and affording him an opportunity of defending his right. I think it will be accepted by every hon. member in this House, and particularly, by the lawyers, that the right to vote is property, and that no citizen of this country, whether he was born in- this country or elsewhere, once he has become a British subject, should be deprived of property or civil rights without being given notice, and an opportunity of saying to the court before whom he is called, the reason why he should not be so deprived. This enumerator does not sit publicly. The man who is deprived of his vote does not know where the enumerator is sitting. The only thing he knows is, when he goes to the poll to cast his ballot, that his name is not on the list, and he will then discover that at some place and at some time this enumerator struck his name off the list. There should, therefore, be something in this Bill a little more explicit than we have now by which it would be known to men who are likely to be struck off the list, where this official will be sitting, and that when that official goes over the list and comes across names he intends to strike off, he should serve notice on such men that on a certain day he intends to deal with the question whether or not they shall remain on the list.
They can then appear before him and give such answer as they may have. Eyen if their reasons would not change the mind of the enumerator these men, would feel more satisfied, and it would be more along the lines of British practice if they were given notice. There is nothing in the Bill to enable the enumerator to do that. There is no provision as to where the enumerator is to come from. I have no great objection to any man in my county beingx appointed an enumerator, but I think it would be better that enumerators be appointed within the county. I would not care that enumerators from the westfern part of the province should be brought down to my county, and I am sure the people of the western portion of Nova Scotia would object to meh being brought down from Cape Breton to be enumerators in the western part of the province. Provision should also be made that enumerators should be residents of good standing in the county in which they are to operate. They are ap-

pointed in a lump number by the Governor in Council. Then the returning officer distributes them to the different parts of the county. The town of Sydney Mines is divided into six or seven polling divisions. Will there be an enumerator for each of those polling divisions?

An unwarrantable attack, I say, upon a gallant soldier, Colonel Currie of the 48th Highlanders. One would have thought that a man who boasted of his Gaelic descent, and of his Scottish birthright, would have been the last to stand up in a public assembly and attack a member of the gallant 48th. There seems to be the bitterness of gall there. My immediate object in referring to the matter is to say to hon. gentlemen of this House that the attack is absolutely without foundation and entirely unworthy any hon. gentleman to make in this House against a soldier who has been under fire at the front with his men, day in and day out, at the risk of his life. A man who has shown the intrepidity that Colonel Currie has shown should not be attacked in such an unwarrantable manner on the floor of this House from personal or any other motives.
I have seen not only one, but two letters from the front from men who have served under Colonel Currie. I wish I had them here, because it was with great pleasure that I read them. One was from a private in the ranks who had seen some of the attacks made against Colonel Currie in the press of this country and throughout, the world, and he said that the attacks were without foundation, and that the men who have served under Colonel Currie loved him so much "they would follow him to hell." To hear a gallant officer defamed in this House in that way makes my blood boil, and I think it is only right that I should tell the House what I have learned from letters from the front.

. With regard to the general attitude of hon. gentlemen apposite, as I have listend to this debate I have -been struck by one thing above all others, and that is that some lion, members opposite have shown no love for the soldier's wife, and mother, and sister and daughter. Others with a higher patriotic spirit have maintained a -splendid respectful silence. This House -has witnessed -an -attack on a soldier -and his near relatives. We have witnessed a deliberate attempt in the face of public opinion in -Canada to give to the wife of the slacker and the wife of the a'ien enemy -a -status equal to that of the wife of the -so-ldier who -is fighting for the Empire. I do not know why that should *be. Have we descended so far in the realm of party politics that the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) will -stand up in this House and say, -as he did the other night, that a party in this House will hear from the -alien enemy wife and widow -and sister in -thunder tones? He mistakes the patriotic women of Canada. There i-s no more loyal woman in the world than the patriotic women of C-anada, who are glad to -see the soldier's wife, and daughter, -and mother, and sister, who have m-ade the greater -sacrifice getting the vote. The women of Canada who have knitted -socks -and made comforts for the soldier have displayed -a patriotic spirit right through that would have been an inspiration for the hon. member for St. John if he had felt like coming u-p -to the high standard these women have set. These wo-men -are proud that the sold-ier'-s women relatives are being given a preference in the matter -of voting.
I was very -much amused at my -hon. friend fro-m North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) taking the attitude he did after he had bo-asted -so much of being Gaelic. Why, the record of Scotchmen the world over is one o-f chivalry -and br-av-ery; there never wa-s a Scotchman in the days of old who would have voted against supporting the men -at the front as -my ho-n. friend did; no, not one. They -have alway-s been over the top first, the Black Watch -and the Irish Ennisk-illens. And to hear a Scotchman who has votdd against conscription, against sending -succour to the boys who -are fighting in France and Flanders for his liberty in this country-to hear him boasting of his Gaelic ancestry and indulging in -a tirade of abuse -against an officer who has seen service at the front, is a very -painful thing for me to have to listen to. There are grandfathers in my county of the boys who are gone to the front, old men who came into the county in the pioneer days, who pioneered the farms, and built up their homes, but have never been naturalized because in the early days no one thought of it. Some of them took an oath of allegiance. Now because these men happen to have been bom in Germany, although their sons and grandsons are fighting for you, Mr. Chairman, and for the country at large, you are going to disfranchise them under this Bill. A finer and more loyal body of citizens never lived in any country in the world. Their sons are as British, and even much more British, than some men in this House. They are absolutely intrepid and fearless. They iiave gone forward and have done their duty like soldiers, and have died like men. They have won honours which have reflected glory upon the Dominion of Canada. Why could not the grandfathers of those boys be naturalized in some way? Why should they not be recognized? It is true there are numbers in the province of Ontario, and there are some in other provinces, who have sons and grandsons enlisted, and who are not able to vote. The hon. member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy) is not speaking strictly correctly when he states they are disfranchised by this Bill. No man who has a son or grandson at the front is disfranchised no matter what race he belongs to. No man	who has
a brother in the overseas forces is disfranchised by this Bill, no matter what race or country he comes from. The trouble is there are men who, although they may have exercised the ballot, have not been naturalized, consequently they are not able to vote. They have never been legally qualified, and they are not now. Their statue is not changed in the least. The law as to them is precisely as it was before. To meet the suggestion as the hon. member for North Perth stated it would involve the giving of the franchise to other than British subjects in the country. In the case of military voters, those who have gone overseas and are fighting in France, though we went, as far as we believe any Government in the world has gone, and as far as we believe we could, we did not go so far ae to enfranchise even the soldieT himself if he were not a British subject. Consequently, I think it would be going too far, if we were now to entertain the idea of enfranchising the relatives of the soldiers who may not be British subjects. They labour under a disability at the present time which I freely admit is in certain cases a hardship. In many instances, through no fault of their own they have not been naturalized; in many cases they believed they were naturalized, and they lived for years having taken some oath of allegiance, and in the sincere belief that they were naturalized, and they exercised all the functions of citizenship. Many of them made the very best citizens in this country. However, when the war broke out, the subject of naturalization became a live one, and men began to inquire. It was ascertained that very many who thought they were naturalized as a matter of fact were never naturalized at all, and very many more who had paid no attention whatever to the subject became alive to the conviction that they were not really British citizens at 'all. After the outbreak of the war the British Government sent a despatch to this Government to the effect that they
in Great Britain were not naturalizing any alien enemy subjects, and suggesting that we follow the same practice in Canada. We were in this position: We had a Naturalization Act which had been on our statute-book for years, which prescribed the conditions of naturalization as three years' residence, and certain oaths, etc., and which placed the power to naturalize in the hands of the judges. That Act was still in force. Men had come to this country on the faith of that Act .and had assumed duties of citizenship relying upon it being carried out. Consequently, we did not feel we should interfere with the exercise of the right of our judges to enfranchise under the Act, and we so notified the British Government. But aside from that restriction, aside from that limitation, we have abided by the practice followed by the British Government and the request they made of us. The result is this; that some judges under the old Act have granted naturalization; others have refused it. The practice in the province of Ontario, following the decision of Chief Justice Meredith, 'has been to refuse naturalization. Consequently, in the province of Ontario, there has.been no naturalization by the judges under the old Act, and there has been no naturalization under the new Act by the Secretary of State, on account of the understanding with the British Government.

No reason can be given for giving votes to the relatives of those who are in the naval service and not giving them to those who have joined the expeditionary forces and who still remain in Canada. The memorandum, which has been prepared by Mr. Des-barats, the deputy minister, is as follows: The War-Time Elections Act.

subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
It is true, as the Solicitor General suggests, that we have rule 17A, but we have also a special rule, rule 56, bearing upon a particular point. Rule 56, which has not been repealed, says :
All amendments made In committee are reported by the chairman to the House, which shall receive the same forthwith. After report the Bill is open to debate and amendment, before it is ordered for a third reading. But when a Bill is reported without amendment it is forthwith ordered to be read a third time at such time as may be appointed by the House.
It is argued by the Solicitor General that that rule is inconsistent with rule 17 A. When we have a rule dealing with general matters and also a special rule stating what shall take place in a particular instance, that special rule would not be overruled by the general rule. If the House had intended when it adopted rule 17 A to repeal rule 56 it would have done so. But it did not do so; therefore, rule 56 is still in force. I think that if there is any doubt in the matter Your Honour should decide in favour of rule 56, because the rights of the minority in this House are very much restricted. It should be borne in mind also that this Government, by virtue of its majority, can declare anything to be carried. I await Your Honour's interpretation of the rule in full confidence that the House will support your decision. It seems to me to be clear that under rule 56 the Bill is now open to debate and amendment.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: THE HOUSE IN COMMITTEE ON THE WARTIME ELECTIONS ACT-RULE 17B APPLIED.
speechtext:
The point of order raised by the member for St. John is, indeed, a most important one; I have had occasion to give the matter consideration within the past few days. As a matter of fact, the point has already been settled by decision of the House, to be found on page 5374 of Hansard of August 29, 1917. Rule 56 is in conflict with rule 17 A, but rule 56 was in the rule book and was prior in point of time to rule 17 A, which, overriding ail other rules, was designed specifically for the purpose of restricting debate. If the interpretation placed upon the rule by the member for St. John were sustained, the express object which the House had in mind when it enacted rule 17 A would be defeated. Notwithstanding that, I am cognizant of the import of the point raised by my hon.
friend. It is very clear in my mind that rule 17 A must prevail; that it must override rule 56 and that, therefore, it is not open to the hon. gentleman to enter into a discussion at this stage of the proceedings. In any case the discussion could take place only on the motion which I now propose to put: that the amendments be now read the second time and concurred in; and under rule 17 A that motion is not debatable.
It is moved by Mr. Meighen, seconded by Mr. Hazen, that the said amendments be now read the second time and concurred in. Is it the pleasure of the House to adopt the motion?
